verdict.what_management_expects: Stated only indirectly: CV and PV housed in two separate listed entities, each with its own board, leadership and dividend (Rs. 3 + Rs. 4 vs Rs. 6 before); TMPV consolidating PV, EV and JLR under one automotive segment, with a net-cash India business (Rs. 7,000 Cr) giving flexibility to fund its product investment cycle while JLR carries Rs. 33,000 Cr net debt.
verdict.gaps: No value-unlock, focus, valuation or synergy argument; no demerger costs/benefits beyond stamp duty; no dis-synergies, debt-allocation logic, or any investor, lender or partner request.

verdict.rationale: Across the three transcripts tagged here (the Q3/9M FY26 call of February 10, 2026, which appears twice, and the Q4/FY26 call of May 21, 2026) and all 27 filings, Embassy Developments Limited (EMBDL/EDL) never announces, proposes or explains a separation, demerger, spin-off or carve-out of any of its own businesses — the stated direction of travel is the opposite, consolidation: FY26 was 'the first full year of the merged platform following the integration of NAM Estates and the erstwhile Indiabulls Real Estate Limited under the unified Embassy Developments brand', accounted for as a reverse merger under Ind AS 103 with NAM as accounting acquirer and EDL as accounting acquiree. The only separation management actually explains is historical and belongs to the predecessor group: a court-approved demerger in FY2010-11 that separated the power business, Sinnar Thermal Power Limited (STPL), from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group / real estate business, after which STPL was controlled by the unrelated Rattan India Group (Rattan India Power Limited and Rattan India Enterprises Limited) and 'was not under the control of the Company'. Management raised that 15-year-old separation only because a lender used its surviving guarantee framework against EDL: Canara Bank (successor to Syndicate Bank, which had sanctioned facilities aggregating Rs 1,444.00 million to STPL) claimed Rs 372 crore under a 2010/2011 corporate guarantee tied to an equity-infusion undertaking and filed a Section 7 IBC application; NCLT admitted CIRP on December 9, 2025, NCLAT stayed it on December 11, 2025, and on May 4, 2026 NCLAT quashed it, holding 'that no deed of guarantee existed and that the application was barred under Section 10A of the IBC', after which EDL exited the NSE ASM framework on May 6, 2026. EDL's defence rested on the separation itself: the obligation was an equity infusion and not 'debt', it was limited, contingent and secondary to the Rattan India Group post-demerger, and against a required infusion of Rs 2,454 crore the Rattan India Group had already infused Rs 3,026 crore, so no obligation survived. The forward-looking corporate actions in the window are consolidations and disposals rather than business separations: the Spero Properties and Services amalgamation into Equinox India Infraestate (appointed date April 1, 2025), and repeated voluntary strike-offs of non-operational subsidiaries (Ariston Investments, Lenus Constructions, Sentia Constructions, Equinox India Multiplex Services, Mariana Constructions, Apesh Real Estate, Varali Real Estate, Devona Infrastructure, Dev Property Development) undertaken 'to simplify its corporate structure and reduce administrative and compliance costs'. The closest thing to separating a business is asset-level monetisation: the April 11, 2026 share purchase agreement to sell 100% of Sepset Real Estate Limited — owner of the 'Mega Mall' commercial project in Jodhpur, which contributed Rs 18.55 crore of income (0.85%) and negative net worth of Rs 114.07 crore — to Pen India Limited for Rs 100 crore cash, plus the flagged disposal of non-core, non-contiguous Panvel parcels, possible disposal of the 500+ acre Sohna land where only ~75 acres is developable, and the Nashik 'debonding' exercise to strip SEZ status from ~1,500 acres so it can be sold as industrial plots. One potential separation was explicitly considered and dropped: management 'had a thought about forward purchasing' Embassy East Business Park (Phase 1, 2.7 msf, GDV ~Rs 3,100 crore) with Embassy REIT and chose instead to build it out and defer any exit-versus-hold decision by three to four years, while targeting an 80:20 residential:commercial mix moving toward 70:30. No investor, lender, banker or partner in these texts asks for a separation; the asks are presales and collections delivery, a lower cost of debt (14.8% down toward 10%), lower leverage (0.3x net debt/equity), reduction of the promoter pledge (68% back toward 47-48%), and clarity on when the reported P&L turns positive.
verdict.evolution: February 10, 2026 (Q3/9M FY26, the first earnings call as the merged entity): the only separation discussed is the FY2010-11 court-approved demerger of the power business (STPL) from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group, surfaced purely as context for Canara Bank's Rs 372 crore Section 7 claim and the NCLAT stay, while a possible REIT carve-out of Embassy East Business Park is disclosed as considered and dropped in favour of building it out. Between calls the separation-adjacent activity is disposal, not demerger: the April 11-12, 2026 sale of Sepset Real Estate (Mega Mall, Jodhpur) to Pen India for Rs 100 crore, continuing subsidiary strike-offs (March 10/16, April 6/21, June 10, 2026), and the May 4, 2026 NCLAT order quashing CIRP on the merits of the old demerger-era guarantee. May 21, 2026 (Q4/FY26): the legacy separation is closed out as a won litigation, and management reframes portfolio pruning — monetising scattered/unmutated erstwhile-Indiabulls land, entertaining offers on Sohna, and 'debonding' the ~1,500-acre Nashik SEZ — as non-core exits rather than any business separation. Nothing in the August-October 2026 filings (Rs 1,020 crore and Rs 105 crore NCDs, the Rs 362.62 crore promoter warrant issue fully converted by October 30, 2026) introduces a separation; they raise and recapitalise within one entity.

points.quote: as part of the Company's ongoing initiative to simplify its corporate structure and reduce administrative and compliance costs

points.point: Management's own strategic framing is consolidation of two platforms into one listed developer with ~38 msf and a 3,100+ acre land bank across 8 cities — the stated rationale is scale and access, the inverse of a separation thesis.
points.quote: This merger was not simply about consolidation. It was a deliberate step to create a stronger, more resilient and future ready listed real estate platform, one with institutional scale, deeper operating capabilities and broader access to high quality markets.

verdict.what_management_expects: No separation benefits are claimed, because none is planned. For the disposals they do describe: unlocked value, a stronger balance sheet and capital redeployed into core markets; non-core land exits and Nashik debonding to raise realisable value; lower cost of debt (14.8% toward 10%) and net debt/equity near 0.3x; ~47-50% net cash surplus margins; simpler structure cutting compliance cost.

verdict.rationale: The separation is not HSCL shedding a business — it is Dalmia Bharat Refractories Limited (DBRL) demerging its Tyre Business (Birla Tyres, the Balasore plant, with all assets, liabilities, contracts, employees, brands and trademarks) into HSCL as a going concern on an as-is-where-is basis, with Appointed Date 1 October 2026, approved by HSCL's Board on 21 September 2026 on the recommendation of its Audit Committee and Committee of Independent Directors. The board's stated logic is two-sided: 'more focused ownership and robust operating structure for the Demerged Undertaking' while 'enabling each of the Companies to deploy its management attention, capital and resources towards businesses aligned with its respective strategic capabilities and long-term objectives' — i.e. DBRL goes back to refractories, HSCL takes the tyre asset it has effectively been building since the October 2023 resolution in which it was strategic partner to DBRL as resolution applicant. The problem it solves is structural, not operational: Birla Tyres was manufactured and carried on DBRL's balance sheet while HSCL's wholly-owned Himadri Clean Energy merely bought and resold the tyres, so HSCL booked the revenue but no tyre P&L — Anurag Choudhary said in Jul 2026 the business was not yet EBITDA positive and 'once it becomes part of Himadri, then the numbers will come', and in Apr 2026 refused volume/realisation disclosure because 'we have not consolidated'. The six rationale heads in the filing are: forward integration of the tyre business with HSCL's carbon black and advanced carbon materials; leveraging HSCL's material expertise, R&D, manufacturing and customer relationships for tyre product customisation; synergies across raw-material sourcing, product development, manufacturing, logistics, distribution, market development, shared services and customer engagement; direct ownership and control to coordinate capacity utilisation, modernisation, product expansion and distribution build-out; strategic and financial flexibility to align investment, funding and capacity expansion with group strategy; and long-term growth and value creation. The scale is small for HSCL — demerged turnover of INR 149.31 crores at 31 March 2026, just 3.39% of HSCL's FY26 revenue — and the consideration is non-cash: 1 HSCL share of Re 1 for every 260 DBRL shares of Rs 10, on a valuation dated 20 September 2026 by SSPA & Co and CA Manish Gadia, with a fairness opinion from Jajodia Equity Advisors; only 1,76,462 new shares are issued, moving HSCL promoters from 52.49% to 52.47% and public from 47.51% to 47.53%, with DBRL's own shareholding unchanged. The direct-ownership point matters because the tyre plan is capital-hungry: phased conversion of Truck-and-Bus-Bias capacity to OTR over three years, Rs 500 crores of Birla Tyres capex in FY27 alone, PCR commissioning by FY28 for EV/SUV, 400+ SKUs under development, and a Rs 3,000 crore top-line target in four to five years. Notably, the filing's forward-integration claim sits against management's repeated earlier statement that HSCL would not sell carbon black to Birla Tyres because each business runs its own P&L and HSCL realises more selling speciality black elsewhere.
verdict.evolution: The idea was explicitly ruled out on the 18 Jul 2025 call, when Sanjesh Jain asked when the manufacturing entity would come inside Himadri and Choudhary replied there was no intention as of that date — HSCL's role was a Rs 300 crore investment for a Rs 3,400 crore asset, with Himadri Clean Energy acting as marketing arm buying tyres from DBRL. On the 24 Oct 2025 and 21 Jan 2026 calls the structure's awkwardness surfaced in questions about consol-minus-standalone revenue and tyre EBITDA, and Choudhary first hinted at change: buying from Dalmia and reselling meant 'no positive or negative impact as such as of now. But looking forward, the things will change.' By 27 Apr 2026 he was deferring all tyre disclosure to 'once we consolidate', and on 16 Jul 2026 he stated plainly that Birla Tyres sits on Dalmia Refractory's balance sheet and the numbers would come once it becomes part of Himadri. Two months later, a 18 September 2026 board-meeting notice and the 21 September 2026 board approval formalised the demerger with Appointed Date 1 October 2026 — no earnings call ever discussed the scheme itself.

points.point: The scheme demerges DBRL's Tyre Business — all assets, liabilities, contracts, employees, brands, trademarks, licences and properties — into HSCL as a going concern, on an as-is-where-is basis, with Appointed Date 1 October 2026.
points.quote: The Scheme, inter-alia, provides for demerger by way of transfer and vesting of the Tyre Business of DBRL ("Demerged Undertaking") from DBRL to HSCL as a going concern, on an as is where is basis, and the consequent issuance of Resulting Company New Shares (as defined in the Scheme) by HSCL to the eligible shareholders of DBRL in accordance with the Share Entitlement Ratio.

points.point: The board's core rationale is focus on both sides: a cleaner operating structure for the tyre business and each company directing management attention and capital to its own strategic capabilities.
points.quote: The Board of Directors, after considering the nature of the Demerged Undertaking, its future requirements, respective strengths and strategic objectives of Resulting Company, is of the view that the proposed Demerger would provide a more focused ownership and robust operating structure for the Demerged Undertaking, while enabling each of the Companies to deploy its management attention, capital and resources towards businesses aligned with its respective strategic capabilities and long-term objectives.

points.point: Head (a) is forward integration: folding tyres into HSCL's carbon black and advanced carbon materials platform to extend its presence across the tyre value chain.
points.quote: The Demerger will enable the Resulting Company to integrate the Tyre Business with its existing carbon black and advanced carbon materials business, thereby strengthening its presence across the tyre value chain.

points.point: Head (d) names the structural fix directly — direct ownership and control, in place of the buy-and-resell arrangement, so capacity utilisation, modernisation, product expansion and distribution can be run as one plan.
points.quote: The Demerger will provide the Resulting Company with direct ownership and control of the Tyre Business, enabling coordinated capacity utilisation, modernisation, product expansion and development of market and distribution channels.

points.point: Heads (c) and (e) list synergies across sourcing, product development, manufacturing, logistics, distribution, shared services and customer engagement, plus flexibility to align funding and capacity expansion with group strategy.
points.quote: The integration is expected to create synergies across raw material sourcing, product development, manufacturing, logistics, distribution, market development, shared services and customer engagement, thereby enhancing operating efficiencies.

points.point: The acquired business is tiny relative to HSCL — INR 149.31 crores of FY26 turnover, 3.39% of HSCL's revenue — which is notably below the INR 187 crores of tyre top line management cited on the April 2026 call.
points.quote: Turnover of the Demerged Undertaking as on 31 March 2026, was INR 149.31 crores, which constitutes 3.39% of total turnover of Resulting Company in the immediately preceding financial year / based on financials of last financial year (i.e. for year ended 31 March 2026).

points.point: No cash changes hands; DBRL shareholders get 1 HSCL share of Re 1 for every 260 DBRL shares of Rs 10, issuing only 1,76,462 new shares so HSCL promoters move 52.49% to 52.47% and DBRL's own shareholding is unchanged.
points.quote: "I (One) fully paid-up equity shares of face value of INR 1 (one) each of the Resulting Company shall be issued and allotted for every 260 (Two Hundred Sixty) fully paid-up equity shares of face value of INR 10 (ten) each held in the De merged Company ("Share Entitlement Ratio'').

points.point: Bhavin Chheda asked whether the INR 127 crore quarterly tyre revenue was EBITDA positive; Choudhary said not yet and explained the reason is structural — the P&L sits with Dalmia while HSCL only recognises resale revenue through a subsidiary.
points.quote: So now Birla Tyres is reflected on Dalmia Refractory balance sheet.

points.point: The direct-ownership case is capital-led: Rs 500 crores of Birla Tyres capex in FY27 within a Rs 2,000 crore group programme, phased TBB-to-OTR conversion over three years, PCR by FY28, 49 distributors and 1,000+ dealers, EBITDA breakeven targeted in FY27 and Rs 3,000 crores of top line in four to five years.
points.quote: We will continue this trajectory and in next 4 years to 5 years the target is to reach INR3,000 Crores of top line in Birla tyres.

points.point: Asked by Dhruvin Kadakia for a tyre volume and realisation break-up, Choudhary refused on the ground that the business was not consolidated — the disclosure gap the demerger closes. FY26 tyre top line was INR 187 crores.
points.quote: Once we consolidate, then we can discuss this.

points.point: Viraj Sanghvi asked the EBITDA margin on the INR 60 crore quarterly tyre revenue; Choudhary described the Himadri Clean Energy buy-from-Dalmia-and-resell model as margin-neutral and flagged a coming change.
points.quote: So we don't have any positive or negative impact as such as of now. But looking forward, the things will change.

points.point: Sanjesh Jain asked directly when the manufacturing entity would come inside Himadri; management ruled it out at that time, describing Himadri Clean Energy only as the marketing arm buying tyres from DBRL.
points.quote: No, there is no intention as such now as of date of its coming into Himadri.

points.point: The economics management cited for the tyre entry — a sub-10% entry price on the asset base, plus Rs 250-300 crores of additional capex in FY26 continuing for three years — and the B2C rationale of a 40-year brand as a launching pad.
points.quote: Basically , our investment has been only Rs. 300 crores for an asset worth Rs. 3,400 crores.

points.point: The forward-integration claim in the Scheme sits against management's original position that HSCL would sell no carbon black to Birla Tyres, because each business runs its own P&L and HSCL realises more selling speciality black elsewhere.
points.quote: However, it is important to note that Himadri will not be selling any carbon black to Birla Tyres.

verdict.what_management_expects: For HSCL: direct ownership and control of Birla Tyres, forward integration with carbon black, synergies in sourcing, R&D, manufacturing, logistics and distribution, and flexibility to fund the OTR conversion and PCR build — plus visible tyre P&L. For DBRL: focus on its remaining business with shareholding unchanged. Dilution is negligible, 1,76,462 shares.
verdict.gaps: No call ever discussed the demerger: no quantified synergies, no explanation of the Rs149cr versus Rs187cr turnover gap, no NCLT timeline, no investor or lender named as asking.

verdict.segment_name: Tyre Business (Birla Tyres Limited / Himadri Birla Tyre Manufacturer Private Limited) — not a reportable segment in HSCL's disclosures
verdict.unit: ₹ lakh (Annual Report segment notes); presentations use ₹ crore
verdict.measure_notes: No profit or revenue line exists for the tyre business on these pages. HSCL's consolidated segment note reports only 'Carbon materials and chemicals', 'Power' and (FY2026 onward) 'Others — Mining and Other business'; the 'Others' segment is labelled Mining and Other business, not Tyres, so it cannot be taken as the tyre business. Where segment results are given, they represent earnings before other income, finance cost, forex gain/(loss) and tax (i.e. EBIT-like, pre-tax), and segment revenue is split into external and inter-segment. Birla Tyres is mentioned only qualitatively (acquisition in Oct 2023 with DBRL, commencement in Q1FY26, ramp-up) plus a capex figure of Rs. 306 Cr (Presentation May 2026 — page 14; Presentation Jan 2026 — page 19), which is investment, not revenue/profit.

years.source: Annual Report 2024 — page 381 (segments: Carbon materials and chemicals, Power only; no tyre segment)
Annual Report 2025 — page 433 (segments: Carbon materials and chemicals, Power only; no tyre segment)
Annual Report 2026 — page 504 (segments: Carbon materials and chemicals, Power, Others = Mining and Other business; no tyre segment)

latest_quarter.source: Presentation Oct 2026 — pages 15, 41; Presentation May 2026 — page 38 (Birla Tyres slides carry no financials)

verdict.not_found: All tyre-business figures: revenue, operating profit/EBITDA/segment result and PAT, for every year and quarter. Only group-level and Carbon/Power/Others-segment numbers are disclosed.

verdict.rationale: Management framed the demerger as splitting one company that had been doing two businesses with two different investor bases: an asset-heavy business that designs, develops, finances and owns hotels (pension funds, insurance companies betting on inflation, repricing and annuity yield) and an asset-light business that monetises brand, management, loyalty, distribution and technology with almost no capital intensity. Keswani said Lemon Tree had only built hotels in 2004-2007 because owners would not hand their hotels to an unknown brand, and that with the brand now widely recognised (MakeMyTrip's CEO told him 20-25% of occupancy comes from them the moment a Lemon Tree opens) there was no reason to keep owning assets rather than monetise the brand — explicitly the Marriott/Host Hotels and Hilton/Park Hotels playbook. Mechanically (Composite Scheme approved 9 Jan 2026, appointed date 1 April 2026): Carnation Hotels and Hamstede Living merge into LTH; Oriole Dr. Fresh, Canary, Sukhsagar and Manakin merge into Fleur against shares to LTH; and the Demerged Undertaking — 11 operating hotels plus Aurika Shimla under construction, the investment in Arum (Aurika Shillong, 165 rooms) and the entire development capability/team with exclusivity on all future ownership, leasing and development — demerges into Fleur, with 20 Fleur shares for every 311 LTH shares (demerged division turnover Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover; 1,563 operating rooms across 15 hotels per the presentation, 1,820 keys/17 hotels per the press release). A second stated problem was conflict of interest: development capability was moved to Fleur with 'Chinese firewalls' so Fleur shareholders could never feel Lemon Tree was cherry-picking the best assets for itself, and Lemon Tree must refer new acquisition/development opportunities to Fleur. All group debt (about Rs 1,300 crore at demerger, Rs 1,500 crore total borrowings at FY26-end, cost of debt 7.42%) goes to Fleur, leaving Lemon Tree debt-free with only technology and marketing spend, forcing the Board to frame a dividend/shareholder-reward policy. Warburg Pincus (Coastal Cedar Investments B.V.) bought APG's entire 41.09% of Fleur and committed up to Rs 960 crore of primary equity, giving Fleur roughly Rs 3,000 crore of deployable capital at 1:1 debt-equity against 2,500+ rooms under active discussion and Aurika Nehru Place (572 rooms, ~Rs 700 crore); post-scheme LTH shareholders own ~74% of Fleur (32.96% direct plus ~41% through LTH) versus the 59% LTH owns today, and Fleur lists separately for 'transparent price discovery and market-driven valuation of the asset-heavy business'.
verdict.evolution: The idea was first visible as a Fleur listing aspiration in the Nov 2024 call, where Keswani said debt-freedom would come sooner 'if we list Fleur before that' and put an IPO 'within the next 2-3 years at most'; in the Aug 2025 call he disclosed that committees of directors had been set up in both Lemon Tree and Fleur to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via a demerger and listing it, alongside splitting the management teams (Neelendra Singh for LTH from 1 October, Saurabh Shatdal for Fleur), with listing hoped for end-CY2026. In the Nov 2025 call it was 'in process' with a Board subcommittee and a promise of 'some other even more exciting stuff' within three months; the scheme, the Warburg/APG transactions and the 74%/26% shareholding math were announced in the Jan 2026 (15 January) dedicated call with a 12-15 month path to listing. By the Feb 2026 call Keswani confirmed the scheme was effective from 1 April and, responding to Ashish Kumar's request, promised pro forma financials for both entities; those pro formas appeared with the Jun 2026 (29 May) results, where CCI approval (April 2026), Warburg's completed purchase of APG's stake and a longer 12-18 month NCLT-dependent timeline were given, followed by NSE/BSE observation letters on 22 September 2026.

points.point: Asked directly by Kunal Lakhan (CLSA) what was wrong with the old structure, Keswani said the hotel business has two subsets with two different investor types — developers/owners wanting chunky yield and inflation-linked annuity returns versus asset-light investors betting on brand and management — and Lemon Tree was a combination of both.
points.quote: We have actually separated 2 types of businesses. One is asset heavy, long -term appreciating asset, capital intensive. It has a different kind of investor, and this business has a very different kind of investor, and we wanted to actually attract both types of investors.

points.point: He explained the historical accident being corrected: hotels were built only to establish the brand, and with the brand now established the company should monetise it instead of owning assets.
points.quote: We were forced to build hotels to build our brand. But once we build our brand, technically, we do not need hotels because now it is time for Lemon Tree to monetize its brand, which is enormous recall.

points.point: The transfer of the development capability and exclusive development mandate to Fleur was driven by a conflict-of-interest problem — Fleur minorities fearing Lemon Tree would keep the best projects for itself — and was solved with firewalls.
points.quote: Development capability was an issue which was raised in order to maximize Fleur's growth, we did not want shareholders of Fleur to ever feel that Lemon Tree when it recommends any assets was cherry -picking, which means Lemon Tree would say, I have got this very nice asset in Delhi, why should I offer it to Fleur.

points.point: All of Lemon Tree's debt moves to Fleur: Fleur carries roughly Rs 1,300 crore of debt against a ~Rs 900 crore net EBITDA and can borrow another ~Rs 1,300 crore, while Lemon Tree goes to zero debt.
points.quote: Firstly, when this demerger happens, all the debt, including the Lemon Tree's debt, after adjustment is being transferred to Fleur. Fleur will have 100% of our debt and Lemon Tree will have zero debt.

points.point: Keswani justified keeping a ~41% indirect stake in Fleur (challenged by Jinesh Joshi on hold-co discount) as Lemon Tree retaining 'skin in the game' as Fleur's manager, with natural dilution as Fleur raises capital; he quantified that Rs 1,000 crore deployed by Fleur generates ~Rs 350 crore of turnover, Rs 170-180 crore EBITDA and ~Rs 30 crore of fees for Lemon Tree.
points.quote: We felt it was prudent to have significant skin in the game at this stage, which means that going forward, it is very possible that Lemon Tree may dilute or even increase its stake over time; this will obviously be a Board decision .

points.point: Warburg's Rs 960 crore primary commitment plus Fleur's own cash and 1:1 debt gives roughly Rs 3,000 crore to deploy pre-listing against 2,500 rooms in active discussion; Keswani guided Fleur to over Rs 1,000 crore net EBITDA by FY28 and Lemon Tree to 80% EBITDA margin / 60% PAT margin.
points.quote: We have potentially about Rs 3,000 crores available to deploy in this growth before we list.

points.point: Opening the call with pro forma financials for both entities, Keswani described the transaction as simple — Warburg has bought APG's Fleur stake, Lemon Tree transfers 17 hotels and development capabilities in exchange for Fleur shares to LTH shareholders, and Fleur lists.
points.quote: This scheme will result in 2 distinct financially sound businesses.

points.point: He restated the economic outcome for each entity: Lemon Tree debt-free, high-margin, high-ROCE and fee/brand-driven; Fleur the consolidated owner of a fully renovated portfolio, post-scheme India's largest hotel platform by inventory at 5,600 rooms and 39 operational hotels.
points.quote: Post the reorganization , Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt -free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand -related income.

points.point: Shareholder arithmetic: LTH shareholders end up with close to 74% of Fleur (33% direct, ~41% through Lemon Tree) versus the 59% Lemon Tree directly owns in Fleur today, before Warburg's primary infusion; Keswani also said he will cease to be executive at Lemon Tree from March 2027 and focus on Fleur as Executive Chair.
points.quote: Post reorganization , Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own close to 74% of Fleur Hotels, 33% directly and about 41% indirectly through Lemon Tree.

points.point: Answering Achal Kumar, Keswani confirmed Fleur will be brand-agnostic post-demerger and may hand assets to other operators — Lemon Tree has no automatic right to Fleur's hotels and must earn them on results.
points.quote: Yes. But Lemon Tree must be able to deliver best results to get it . Just because Lemon Tree has skin in the game with Fleur does not mean that it has an automatic right to any asset that Fleur develops.

points.point: On capital allocation after the split, Lemon Tree is expected to need almost no capital and move to distributing profits, while Fleur will retain capital for growth rather than pay dividends.
points.quote: Lemon Tree will not need any significant capital other than potentially investments in technology or in marketing and so on. It will be essentially a zero -debt cash accretive company.

points.point: Keswani confirmed the scheme is effective from 1 April and that Lemon Tree becomes debt-free from next year, with all assets and debt going to Fleur and fee income becoming free cash; the Board must decide a dividend policy within six months.
points.quote: What will happen is in the scheme of demerger, all the assets of Lemon Tree, including its debt will be transferred to Fleur. Lemon Tree will immediately effectively be a debt -free company from next year.

points.point: Investors pushed for separate reporting: Ashish Kumar of Infinity Alternatives asked for pro forma financials of both businesses while awaiting the listing, and management agreed to publish them from the next quarter.
points.quote: Now that we have decided on the split of the 2 businesses, what might be helpful is if we can add pro forma financials for both of the assets as they look like so that while we are waiting for the l isting, we do get a good sense of what the numbers are looking like.

points.point: Keswani positioned the asset-light entity as a first in India, with fee income from hotels signed three years earlier only now flowing, and Fleur guided to ~Rs 1,000 crore EBITDA by FY28, its first year as a listed company.
points.quote: And keep in mind that Lemon Tree will be the first fully asset -light brand owning tech and distribution and management company in India, the first.

points.point: The demerger was still with Board subcommittees of both Lemon Tree and Fleur, with management hinting that more than the demerger was being negotiated (the Warburg/APG transactions announced two months later).
points.quote: It is not only the demerger of Fleur, but some other even more exciting stuff, but we will talk about it when the time is right.

points.point: First formal disclosure of the structure: committees of directors in both companies to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via demerger and then list Fleur, with Lemon Tree becoming asset-light and focused on management, brand and technology — described as the global trend in the space.
points.quote: You may have also seen that we have said that a committee of directors has been set up in Lemon Tree and in Fleur to evaluate how we can possibly look at a transfer of assets from Lemon Tree into Fleur through a demerger scheme and then automatically look at how we can list Fleur.

points.point: The separation of management was done first and explicitly for this purpose — Neelendra Singh to run asset-light Lemon Tree from 1 October and Saurabh Shatdal to drive Fleur's asset-heavy growth, with Keswani handholding and moving to strategic oversight.
points.quote: The intent of the leadership change was to get 2 very good people who would then run these two companies independently on a day -to-day basis.

points.point: Keswani drew a hard line on mandates — Fleur builds, buys and leases, Lemon Tree only manages or franchises — and noted that the more Fleur dilutes and raises capital, the more Lemon Tree's economic interest rises via fees (Rs 100+ crore this year, potentially Rs 300-400 crore from Fleur in three years).
points.quote: Fleur's mandate will be to focus on, at the right value, building, buying, or leasing hotels. Lemon Tree's will only be to manage or franchise. Lemon Tree will not lease hotels once the Fleur demerger happens.

points.point: The earliest trace in these calls: a Fleur listing was already seen as the accelerator of deleveraging, with Keswani putting an IPO within 2-3 years at most when asked by Prashant Biyani.
points.quote: I think we are sticking to our guidance that in the next 3 - 3.5 years, we should be debt free , but if we list Fleur before that then we will be debt free that much earlier.

points.point: The 9 Jan 2026 filing states the Board reviewed the business with a view to segregating the asset-heavy ownership/development undertaking from the asset-light management/brand platform, and that the demerged business is self-sustaining and better housed in Fleur; the demerged division's turnover was Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover.
points.quote: Therefore, to achieve operational focus, greater flexibility for capital deployment, and clearer alignment of business objectives, it is proposed under this Scheme to (i) amalgamate Transferor Company 3, Transferor Company 4, Transferor Company 5 and Transferor Company 6 with the Transferee Company; and (ii) demerge and vest the Demerged Undertaking (comprising the Demerged Hotel Properties and the Development Capabilities together with the related undertakings, as defined hereinafter) into the Transferee C ompany, while the Company will continue to focus on the asset -light hotel management support, brand and operations including management support of the hotels transferred to the Transferee Company and other properties.

points.point: A stated purpose is market-driven valuation: Fleur ceases to be LTH's subsidiary and lists, so LTH shareholders participate directly in the asset-heavy business through listed shares rather than through a subsidiary.
points.quote: Following the implementation of the Scheme, the Transferee Company will cease to be a subsidiary of the Company , and its shares will be listed on the Stock Exchanges, enabling transparent price discovery and market -driven valuation of the asset -heavy business.

points.point: The filing also sets out structural clean-up and partner-flexibility objectives: merging two wholly owned subsidiaries into LTH to remove layering and cost, and creating a structure that lets Fleur bring in investors or co-development partners per project without touching LTH's brand operations.
points.quote: To create a flexible structure enabling the Transferee Company to attract investors or co -development partners for specific hotel projects, without affecting Company's brand operations or control over strategic decisions.

points.point: Continuity is contractually locked: every hotel amalgamated into or demerged to Fleur stays under Lemon Tree Hotel Operating Agreements (existing ones amended/restated and extended from the Appointed Date), and LTH must refer new acquisition/development opportunities to Fleur and drop them if Fleur declines.
points.quote: Further, all the hotels amalgamated with or demerged into the Transferee Company will continue to be managed and operated by the Company under Hotel Operating Agreements and, the existing Hotel Operating Agreements with the Transferee Company and its subsidiaries shall be amended and/or restated, inter alia, to reflect the revised terms as detailed in the Scheme, and the Company shall refer new hotel acquisition or development opportunities to the Transferee Company and shall not pursue them if declined, except for hotel operations/franchise arran gements through third parties.

points.point: The Shareholders' Agreement with Warburg gives Fleur the exclusive global right to own, lease and develop hospitality assets, Investor/LTH affirmative consent on reserved matters, up to 3 Investor and 3 LTH directors with Keswani as non-retiring executive chairman, and the right to inject up to Rs 960 crore of primary capital.
points.quote: The Agreement provides Fleur t he exclusive right to own, lease and develop hospitality assets globally, with LTHL being entitled to undertake key money arrangements, in the manner as mutually agreed.

points.point: The 22 Sept 2026 filing records receipt of NSE 'no objection' and BSE 'no adverse observation' letters under Regulation 37, valid six months, with NCLT, shareholder and creditor approvals still pending — the gating item management had flagged as the timing risk.
points.quote: In this regard, we wish to inform you that the Company has received the Observation Letter s with 'no objection ' from the NSE and 'no adverse observations' from the BSE on September 22, 2026 vide their respective letters , pursuant to Regulation 37 of the Listing Regulations , in relation to the Scheme .

verdict.what_management_expects: Lemon Tree: debt-free, fee/brand/tech-only, EBITDA margin from ~60% pro forma to 70-80% steady state, ~60% PAT margin, high ROCE, free cash funding dividends. Fleur: India's largest owner (5,600 rooms, 39 hotels), net EBITDA Rs 850 crore FY27 and Rs 1,000+ crore FY28, ~48%+ post-fee margins, Warburg-backed capital for 2,500+ rooms, capital growth not dividends, and separately listed for market valuation.
verdict.gaps: Absolute valuation of the demerged undertaking and Warburg's price for APG's stake, Fleur's issue price, hold-co discount size, post-demerger ROE, and fate of the two retained leases.

verdict.segment_name: Fleur Hotels Limited (formerly Fleur Hotels Private Limited) — the Demerged Undertaking / hospitality asset platform (asset-heavy hotel-ownership business)
verdict.unit: ₹ crore (presentations) | ₹ lakhs (annual report notes) — no Fleur-level figures given in either unit
verdict.measure_notes: No separate profit or revenue line exists for Fleur. Both the consolidated and standalone annual reports state the Group/Company is in a single Hoteliering business with 'no reportable segment' under Ind AS 108 (AR2024 p162/p200, AR2025 p200/p240, AR2026 p192/p235), so there is no segment revenue, segment result, EBIT or EBITDA for Fleur. The quarterly presentations report only Lemon Tree consolidated P&L (total revenue, Net EBITDA, PBT before exceptional items, PAT) and a Keys Hotels sub-column — Fleur is not a reported line. The only Fleur-specific amounts on these pages are management/franchise fees LTH earns FROM Fleur (₹22.6 cr in Q1 FY27, up 6% YoY — Presentation Aug 2026 p5; ₹22.1 cr in Q2 FY27, up 11% YoY and ₹44.7 cr in H1 FY27 — Presentation Nov 2026 p5; ₹95.8 cr in FY26, up 8% YoY — Presentation Jun 2026 p5). These are the parent's fee income, not Fleur's own revenue, operating profit or PAT, so they are not reported as Fleur financials here.

verdict.not_found: All Fleur-level figures: revenue, operating profit/EBITDA and PAT, for every year and quarter. Pages carry no segment disclosure and no Fleur standalone statements — only fees LTH earns from Fleur.

verdict.rationale: There are no earnings-call transcripts on file, so the 'why' can only be reconstructed from the filings, where management states a single rationale in two places: the moves 'form a part of internal restructuring and consolidation of the AI / Technology business under the Company's vertical "Brahma"', which 'is expected to leverage the brand value and provide additional revenue streams', and more generally are 'internal restructuring within the group to streamline the business operations'. Mechanically, the AI/technology business (ex-Prime Focus Technologies Limited, renamed Brahma AI Services India Limited; Metaphysic Limited renamed Brahma AI Services UK Limited; DAX Cloud ULC renamed Brahma AI Canada Inc.; DNEG Creative renamed Brahma AI India Technologies) is being pulled out from under the VFX chain and parked under Brahma AI Holdings Limited (Jersey, 90.20% held by Double Negative Holdings), which already holds Metaphysic Inc., acquired 14 February 2025 for USD 130 million (Rs 111,100.30 Lakhs) settled in subsidiary shares and generating Rs 96,942.67 Lakhs of goodwill (later Rs 6,399.09 Lakhs more). The legacy services are simultaneously pushed the other way into the DNEG post-production chain: Brahma India's TCS business and Restoration business were slump-sold as a going concern to DNEG India Media Services Limited for INR 26.5 Crores (FY25 turnover INR 102.62 Crores, 2.85% of consolidated turnover; net worth INR 23.86 Crores, 2.38%), and 100% of Prime Focus Technologies Inc. (PFT US) moves from Brahma India to DNEG S.a.r.l. for around USD 21 Million, while proprietary software and associated rights move from Brahma India (INR 75.2 Crores) and PFT US (US$ 3.44 Million) to Brahma AI ME Ltd. The headline step is DNEG S.a.r.l. selling the entire shareholding of Brahma India (92.23% held by DNEG plus 7.77% from other shareholders) to Brahma AI Holdings Limited for USD 90.09 Million; FY2025-26 figures put Brahma India at INR 328.72 Crores turnover (7.03% of consolidated) and INR 278.63 Crores net worth (10.95%), and PFT US at INR 99.74 Crores turnover (2.13%) and INR 1.04 Crores net worth (0.04%). Management insists nothing leaves the group — 'PFT US and Brahma India will continue to be part of the group and will continue to be step-down subsidiaries of the Company' — and that the PFT US share issuance 'does not involve any fresh infusion of capital', being only a conversion of an inter-company loan and optionally convertible redeemable preference shares. No filing names any investor, lender or partner as having asked for the separation; the only contemporaneous external pressure disclosed is the Raspalfa/Reliance Alpha Section 7 insolvency petition for Rs 353.79 crores (NCLT admission 6 May 2026, stayed by NCLAT 12 May 2026, Rs 35,379.75 Lakhs deposited, Bombay High Court suit withdrawn as settled 4 August 2026) and a USD 500 Mn refinancing of foreign-subsidiary debt to June 2029.
verdict.evolution: The separation starts before the Brahma label exists: in the quarter ended 30 June 2024 PFL sold its entire PFT shareholding down to DNEG S.a.r.l. for Rs 69,302.55 Lakhs (exceptional gain Rs 21,621.18 Lakhs), and on 14 February 2025 Metaphysic Inc. was acquired for USD 130 million under Brahma AI Holdings Limited; through FY26 the technology entities were renamed 'Brahma'. The September 2025 preferential issue (46,26,69,444 shares at Rs 120, Rs 5,55,203.33 Lakhs, mostly a 2,561:100 swap of DNEG subsidiary shares) pulled DNEG up into the listed company, cutting non-controlling interest from Rs 128,432.26 to Rs 45,713.96 Lakhs. The 30 March 2026 audit committee then approved the software assignments to Brahma AI ME Ltd and the TCS/Restoration slump sale to DNEG India, and the 1 April 2026 board/audit committee approved moving PFT US to DNEG and Brahma India to Brahma AI Holdings. On 4 September 2026 the board added an authorised-capital increase to 100 Crore shares and a Rs 3,000 Crore fund-raising enabler, and the 29th AGM on 30 September 2026 passed every one of these as material related-party resolutions, alongside Namit Malhotra's redesignation as Whole-time Director from 7 August 2026.

points.point: March 30, 2026 audit-committee filing gives the only stated rationale: the software assignments from Brahma India (INR 75.2 Crores) and PFT USA (US$ 3.44 Million) to Brahma AI ME Ltd consolidate the AI/technology business under the 'Brahma' vertical.
points.quote: The said software assignment forms a part of internal restructuring and consolidation of the AI / Technology business under the Company’s vertical “Brahma”. This is expected to leverage the brand value and provide additional revenue streams.

points.point: The same rationale is repeated for the slump sale of the TCS business and Restoration business from Brahma India to DNEG India Media Services Limited for INR 26.5 Crores.
points.quote: The said slump sale by Brahma India to DNEG India forms a part of internal restructuring and consolidation of the AI / Technology business under vertical “Brahma”. This is expected to leverage the brand value and provide additional revenue streams.

points.point: The umbrella reason given on both 30 March and 1 April 2026 is streamlining, not value unlock or a listing: the steps are described purely as intra-group restructuring.

verdict.rationale: The materials supplied do not support a reconstruction of a separation rationale, and I will not supply one from memory. No earnings call passages were included — the "CALL PASSAGES" section is empty — so there is no management commentary, no cited numbers, and no statement of who asked for a separation. The one document provided is not a scheme rationale section either: it is a Viyash Scientific Limited (formerly SeQuent Scientific Limited) stock-exchange letter enclosing a Crisil Ratings press release dated January 16, 2026 withdrawing the ratings on Symed Labs Limited's bank facilities. Crucially, the corporate action it documents is the opposite of a separation: it is a two-step consolidation — Symed Labs amalgamated into Viyash Lifesciences Pvt Ltd (deemed effective for Symed on November 27, 2025), and then Viyash amalgamated into SeQuent Scientific Ltd (deemed effective for Viyash on December 16, 2025), under an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated November 18, 2025. The only stated reason for any action in the text is procedural: Crisil withdrew the ratings because Symed ceased to exist post-amalgamation, in accordance with its withdrawal policy. The text does describe the businesses now under one roof — SeQuent, incorporated 1985, an animal health pharmaceuticals company with seven manufacturing facilities globally, five R&D centres and presence in over 100 countries; Viyash, incorporated 2019, a mid-tier API and formulations player with nine Indian plants (~2,000 kilolitre) and one US formulation facility; and Symed, incorporated 1998, with ~50 APIs, four API plants and one R&D centre around Hyderabad, all USFDA-approved and catering exclusively to overseas markets — plus Carlyle's ~53% stake in SeQuent as of March 31, 2025 and its 74% (July 2021) to 100% (July 2024) buildup in Symed. None of that is offered as a reason to separate anything. To answer the actual question, I need the earnings call transcripts and the demerger scheme's rationale clauses.
verdict.evolution: No evolution can be traced: zero call passages were provided, so there are no call dates to sequence. The only dated sequence in the text is the consolidation itself — NCLT Hyderabad order November 18, 2025; Symed into Viyash deemed effective November 27, 2025; Viyash into SeQuent deemed effective December 16, 2025; Crisil rating withdrawal published January 16, 2026. Rating history shows Symed on Crisil A/Watch Developing from October 29, 2024 through October 20, 2025 (previously Crisil A/Stable on August 4, 2023), which is consistent with a pending merger, but no document here explains it.

points.point: The document is a Crisil rating withdrawal, and the stated trigger is a two-step amalgamation (consolidation), not a separation of any business.
points.quote: Crisil Ratings has withdrawn its ratings on the bank facilities of Symed Labs Ltd (Symed), following the amalgamation of Symed with Viyash Lifesciences Pvt Ltd (Viyash) and, subsequently, Viyash's amalgamation with Sequent Scientific Ltd (Sequent).

points.point: The only rationale articulated anywhere in the text is procedural and belongs to the rating agency, not management: Symed ceased to exist, so the ratings lapsed under policy.

No management expectation for margins, capital allocation, valuation re-rating, focus, debt placement, or shareholder entitlement appears, because no earnings call passages were provided and the only filing text is a rating-withdrawal notice whose sole rationale is Crisil's own withdrawal policy.

verdict.rationale: These documents describe no separation, spin-off or demerger — the corporate action is the exact opposite: the amalgamation of the listed subsidiary Dr. Agarwal's Eye Hospital Limited (AEHL) into its parent Dr. Agarwal's Health Care Limited (AHCL), with AEHL dissolved without winding up and its public holders becoming AHCL shareholders. The two businesses were artificially split by geography: AEHL, BSE-listed since 1995 and 72.67% owned by AHCL, held all Tamil Nadu operations (63 facilities, 250+ doctors, 6,19,800+ patients, 72,500+ surgeries; FY25 revenue ₹397.15 cr, EBITDA ₹123.59 cr, PAT ₹54.65 cr), while every new centre outside Tamil Nadu plus Africa sat in AHCL (288 Indian facilities across 14 states/5 UTs and 19 in Africa; FY26 revenue ₹2,080 cr, Ind-AS EBITDA ₹614 cr, PAT ₹168 cr) — Adil Agarwal repeatedly called it 'a clear demarcation.' Management said the merger solves running two listed companies: duplicate compliance cost (two separate statutory auditors, separate filings), GST tax leakage on cross-charges between the entities, duplicated regional/corporate resource loading, and slow decision-making — plus it delivers 'unified capital allocation' so AHCL's holdco cash can be deployed anywhere rather than AEHL having to fund Tamil Nadu capex from its own accruals and debt (₹85.77 cr secured, ₹44.64 cr unsecured at Dec 2025). The capital constraint was concrete: AHCL had to inject ₹70 cr into AEHL by preferential allotment of 1,32,827 shares at ₹5,270 each to pay for the Cathedral Road flagship, chosen over a loan because, in Adil's words, it avoided 'putting any more stress on the balance sheet at the AHCL level'; that lifted promoter holding in AEHL from 71.9% to 72.7%. The ask came from several directions: AHCL itself had promised in its January 31, 2025 IPO prospectus to explore the merger within three years of listing; analysts (Ankit Shah, Harshal Seth, Varun Hemant, Dishant Jain, Rachna Kukreja) pressed for a timeline on every call; and AEHL minority holders demanded the swap be reworked, arguing 15–17 AHCL shares per AEHL share was fairer than the 23:2 offered, that the fairness opinions came from the same bankers (Kotak, Motilal Oswal) the group had just paid on the IPO, and that AEHL had been kept Tamil Nadu-only and never allowed a rights issue or QIP. Terms held firm: PwC and Bansi S. Mehta jointly valued AEHL at ₹4,942–₹5,262 and AHCL at ₹429–₹456 per share (DCF 50%, market price 25%, comparable-company 25%), giving 23 AHCL shares per 2 AEHL shares — a 15% premium to AEHL's 10-day VWAP of ₹4,554 — leaving AEHL public holders 4.6% of the merged entity, AHCL public holding diluted 67.6%→64.5% and promoters ~30.9%, with post-merger net worth of ₹2,225.44 cr versus ₹1,973.87 cr standalone. It cleared every gate: exchange NOCs (NSE Feb 16, BSE Feb 17, 2026), NCLT application March 4, 2026, shareholder approval July 2, 2026 with 99.97% of votes and 99.96% of public votes in favour, NCLT Chennai sanction September 30, 2026, Appointed Date April 1, 2026 and Effective Date November 1, 2026, record date November 18, 2026, authorised capital raised ₹90 cr to ₹110 cr, at a one-time cost of ~₹80 lakhs.
verdict.evolution: It surfaced as an IPO-era promise: on the maiden call (Feb 17, 2025) Adil said bankers had not yet been engaged but pledged a fair valuation and share swap within three years, 'ideally sooner,' while Ankit Shah asked how much dilution to expect. By May 29, 2025 the group was 'speaking to the bankers right now to decide on which bank,' and on Aug 12, 2025 it was 'under consideration… evaluating this further along with advisors,' with the outer limit cut to 1–1.5 years. The dedicated merger call of Aug 28, 2025 fixed the terms (23:2 swap, ₹70 cr preferential allotment, 12–14 month timeline) and drew sustained minority protest that management logged but did not act on; the Nov 2025 call did not mention the merger at all. Thereafter it became pure process reporting — exchange NOC filing (Feb 4, 2026), NCLT first-motion order and July 2, 2026 meetings with completion guided to Q3 (May 21, 2026) — ending in NCLT sanction (Sept 30, 2026) and effectiveness from Nov 1, 2026.

points.point: On AHCL's first call as a listed company, management said no bankers had yet been engaged on the merger but committed to a fair valuation and share swap within three years, framing it as a duty to AEHL's minorities.
points.quote: So from management perspective, it is our fiduciary responsibility to take care of our minority shareholders in the listed subsidiary, which is why when we get down to this process, we will do a fair valuation of both the entities and based on that fair valuation, we will do a share swap of both the entities.

points.point: Adil spelled out the artificial split the merger removes — AEHL holds the Tamil Nadu network and AHCL everything else including Africa — and confirmed banker selection was underway.
points.quote: Outside of the state of Tamil Nadu, which is Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Punjab, all that happens in the holdco which is Dr. Agarwal's Health Care Limited, including Africa.

points.point: Management flagged that AEHL was carrying the group's largest single capex — the Cathedral Road flagship — on its own books, ₹70–80 crore over and above the ₹310 crore group capex, with AEHL's own revenue only ~₹120 crore.
points.quote: Out of the INR 310, INR 60 crores will be for growth capex, plus newer greenfields. The additional INR 70 crores will be over and above this INR 310 crores, which will be spending for the flagship facility.

points.point: The merger was tied explicitly to the DRHP disclosure, with the timeline tightened from the three-year outer limit to 1–1.5 years.
points.quote: So right now, as we had disclosed in the DRHP Varun, the merger of the listed sub with the hold-co is under consideration. Management is now evaluating this further along with advisors. We continue with the endeavor to complete the merger in outer limit of the next 3 years, but we believe in the next 1-1.5 years, we should be able to get this one.

points.point: On the dedicated merger call Adil gave the full rationale — operational and financial efficiencies, unified capital allocation, a stronger balance sheet and a simplified legal and governance framework — calling it a 'long-awaited' simplification.
points.quote: It will enable unified capital allocation, strengthen the balance sheet to support future growth, and provide a simplified legal, regulatory, and governance framework.

points.point: Asked by Binay Singh (Morgan Stanley) to name the duplicated costs, CFO Yashwanth Venkat listed two separate statutory auditors, GST leakage on inter-entity cross-charges, resource optimisation and filing costs.
points.quote: See, in terms of cost synergies, Binay, the main thing is on the compliance costs. One, currently since we have two companies, in terms of the auditors, we have to have two separate auditors for both the companies.

points.point: The ₹70 crore preferential allotment of 1,32,827 AEHL shares at ₹5,270 each was structured as equity rather than an intercompany loan specifically to avoid loading AHCL's balance sheet, deploying holdco cash reserves instead.
points.quote: We believe that instead of us putting any more stress on the balance sheet at the AHCL level, we feel that this will be a better route for us to do a preferential allotment.

points.point: AEHL minority holders, several of 18–30 years' standing, attacked the 23:2 ratio as unfair on revenue, EBITDA, PAT and net worth, with one (Ankur Shah, Quasar Capital) alleging conflict of interest because the fairness-opinion bankers had just been paid on AHCL's IPO.
points.quote: The thing is that it is completely unfair since I am also in the market since last 30 years. I don't know on what metrics, because we can see topline, EBITDA, PAT, growth, net worth, debt, equity on all parameters, it looks completely unfair.

points.point: Siddharth Chandrasekhar pressed on why AEHL had been confined to Tamil Nadu and never allowed to raise equity, arguing AHCL's faster growth was funded by VC and IPO money AEHL was denied; management replied only that the merger now lets AEHL holders participate.
points.quote: Yes, my question is like why we haven't raised any funds in subsidiary, right?

points.point: Management defended the ratio by pointing to the 15% premium over AEHL's ₹4,554 ten-day VWAP, and listed what AEHL holders gain: pan-India growth, a larger clinical talent pool, a larger cash pool and a bigger market-cap company.
points.quote: The swap ratio implies a 15% premium for AEHL over AEHL's 10-day VWAP of INR 4,554 per share.

points.point: The merger became process reporting: NOC filed with the exchanges, NCLT shareholder and creditor meetings expected two to three months later, with COO Rahul Agarwal guiding completion to Q3–Q4 of 2027.
points.quote: So, quickly on the merger update, right now, we have filed for a no-objection certificate from the stock exchanges.

points.point: CFO confirmed exchange observation letters with no adverse objections in Feb 2026 and the NCLT first-motion order convening shareholder and creditor meetings on July 2, 2026; IR guided completion in five to six months. One-time merger expenses of ~₹80 lakhs hit Q4 other expenses.
points.quote: In May 2026, the Honorable NCLT Chennai bench allowed the joint first motion application and directed the convening of meetings of equity shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors of both companies on July 2, 2026.

points.point: The scheme explanatory statement states the consolidation rationale in four heads — operational/financial efficiencies, integrated capital allocation, simplified legal and governance framework, and EPS accretion from year one.
points.quote: The merger will consolidate the businesses of AHCL and AEHL into a single entity, enabling operational and financial efficiencies through streamlined functions and agile decision-making.

points.point: Valuers PwC and Bansi S. Mehta weighted DCF 50%, market price 25% and comparable-company multiples 25%, valuing AEHL at ₹4,942/₹5,262 and AHCL at ₹429/₹456 per share, on projected FY25–FY30 revenue CAGRs of ~22% (AHCL) and ~20.6% (AEHL) versus an industry 12–14%.
points.quote: 23 (Twenty-Three) fully paid-up Equity Shares of face value of ₹1 each of Dr. Agarwal's Health Care Limited for every 2 (Two) fully paid-up Equity Shares of face value of ₹10 each held in Dr. Agarwal's Eye Hospital Limited

points.point: Shareholders approved overwhelmingly despite the call-time protest: 95.91% of capital voted, 99.97% in favour overall and 99.96% of public votes in favour (81,138 shares against). NCLT sanctioned on Sept 30, 2026; effective Nov 1, 2026 with April 1, 2026 appointed date and Nov 18, 2026 record date.
points.quote: Accordingly, the Scheme shall become effective and operative from November 01, 2026 (Effective Date), with the Appointed Date being April 01, 2026.

verdict.what_management_expects: For the single surviving entity (AEHL dissolves): EPS accretion from year one; net worth ₹1,973.87 cr to ₹2,225.44 cr; unified capital allocation letting holdco cash fund Tamil Nadu and pan-India expansion alike; lower compliance costs (one auditor, no GST cross-charge leakage, fewer filings); faster, single-board decision-making. AEHL holders gain pan-India growth, larger talent and cash pools, bigger market cap; AHCL promoters dilute ~1.48%.
verdict.gaps: No separation is explained because none exists — this is a merger. Management never justified the 23:2 ratio on revenue, EBITDA or PAT, never quantified the synergies, and never held the promised separate AEHL-minority valuation call.

verdict.rationale: These texts do not contain any explanation by AIIL management of a separation, demerger or spin-off of one of AIIL's own businesses — there are no earnings-call transcripts on file ('no transcripts on file') and none of the nine filings is a scheme of arrangement for AIIL, so no management rationale, no investor/lender/partner demand and no financial targets for such a separation can be reconstructed from them. The only business separation described anywhere in the material is the splitting of a third party, Wind World (India) Limited (WWIL), between the two members of the consortium that acquired it under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016: the filing of July 28, 2026 states that Inox Neo Energies Limited (INEL, the Lead Member) and/or its affiliates would take (i) the IPP and power sale undertaking and (ii) the operations and maintenance (O&M) business of WWIL, while AIIL and/or its affiliates would take 'certain identified real estate / assets'. AIIL's financial commitment for that identified-asset leg was approximately INR 350 crore, which the October 10, 2026 filing confirms was fully remitted to WWIL (net of TDS filed on WWIL's behalf). That filing also records that the scheme of arrangement forming part of the Resolution Plan was NOT approved by the NCLT in its order of July 27, 2026, so the Consortium used the flexibility in the Resolution Plan to adopt a 'Revised Structure' cleared by the implementation and monitoring committee on August 31, 2026; the debt/equity infusion option that was to go into WWIL was redirected to Vibhav Energy Private Limited (VEPL), an implementation entity of the Lead Member and a subsidiary of Inox Green Energy Services Limited, via a INR 100 crore inter-corporate deposit dated September 28, 2026 that converted on October 9, 2026 into 10,00,00,000 shares, or 25% of VEPL on a fully diluted basis. The stated reason AIIL gives for that 25% stake is only that 'the target entity has strong potential for value creation, and it also aligns with our objective of portfolio diversification' — VEPL had nil turnover in FY2023-24, FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 and negative net worth of INR (0.1) crore at March 31, 2026. The remaining filings concern unrelated capital actions rather than any separation: a 4:1 bonus issue (67,93,80,400 shares, out of Rs. 8,880.02 crore of free reserves/premium at September 30, 2025) approved by the board on November 28, 2025 and by shareholders on December 31, 2025; a Rs. 2,450 crore 0.01% NCRPS private placement to promoter Mentor Capital Limited redeemable at a 6.5% IRR over 15 years, approved November 17, 2025; an ESOP Scheme 2025 of 5,00,000 options including for subsidiary employees; a further Rs. 101.625 crore rights-issue subscription in 88.37%-owned ISARC 'to meet its capital requirement for general business operations'; and the NCLT's July 7, 2026 rejection of AIIL's resolution plan for Vas Infrastructure Limited, with the company stating 'there is no impact on the business operations of the Company'. In short, on these documents alone the question's premise — that AIIL is separating one of its businesses — is not evidenced, and the only documented separation is of WWIL's businesses between AIIL and INEL, driven by the structure of a court-supervised insolvency acquisition rather than by any explained strategic or stakeholder pressure.
verdict.evolution: With no transcripts on file, the only traceable sequence is in the filings: the WWIL resolution plan dated February 13, 2026 (addendum May 20, 2026), intimated February 20, 2026, already envisaged splitting WWIL's IPP/power-sale undertaking and O&M business to INEL and identified real estate/assets to AIIL. The July 28, 2026 filing reported NCLT approval of that plan on July 27, 2026 and restated the INR 350 crore commitment. The October 10, 2026 filing then disclosed that the NCLT did not approve the scheme of arrangement inside the plan, forcing a Revised Structure approved on August 31, 2026, under which AIIL's optional infusion went into INEL's implementation entity VEPL as a INR 100 crore ICD converted to a 25% equity stake on October 9, 2026. Separately, on July 11, 2026 AIIL disclosed the NCLT's July 7, 2026 rejection of its Vas Infrastructure resolution plan, with no impact on operations.

points.point: The separation in these documents is the carve-up of WWIL between the two consortium members: INEL takes the IPP/power-sale undertaking and the O&M business, AIIL takes identified real estate/assets.
points.quote: The Resolution Plan submitted by the consortium of INEL and the Company inter alia envisaged that INEL as the Lead Member and/or its affiliates shall acquire (i) the IPP and power sale undertaking ; and (ii) the operations and maintenance (O&M ) business of WWIL, while the Company and/or its affiliates shall acquire certain identified real estate / assets from WWIL.

points.point: AIIL's leg of the split was sized at approximately INR 350 crore, and the October 10, 2026 filing confirms the full amount was remitted to WWIL net of TDS.
points.quote: The financial commitment of the Company under the Resolution Plan as consideration for the purchase of certain identified assets of WWIL was INR 350,00,00,000 (Indian Rupees Three Hundred and Fifty Crore).

points.point: The scheme of arrangement embedded in the Resolution Plan was rejected by the NCLT in its July 27, 2026 approval order, so the consortium re-engineered the implementation structure, cleared by the implementation and monitoring committee on August 31, 2026.
points.quote: However, since the scheme of arrangement forming part of the Resolution Plan, was not approved by the NCLT vide the NCLT Approval Order, the Consortium revised the transaction structure / structure for implementation of the Resolution Plan (pursuant to such flexibility under the Resolution Plan), which was approved by the implementation and monitoring committee vide its resolution dated August 31, 2026 (“ Revised Structure ”).

points.point: Under the Revised Structure, AIIL's infusion option moved from WWIL to VEPL, an INEL implementation entity: a INR 100 crore ICD dated September 28, 2026 converted on October 9, 2026 into 10 crore shares, 25% of VEPL fully diluted.
points.quote: In terms of the Revised Structure, the Lead Member and the Company had an option to agree on terms and conditions for infusion by the Company of debt / equity in Vibhav Energy Private Limited, one of implementation entities of the Lead Member (“ VEPL”).

points.point: The only stated rationale for AIIL's 25% VEPL stake is value-creation potential and portfolio diversification, despite VEPL reporting nil turnover in each of FY2023-24, FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 and net worth of INR (0.1) crore at March 31, 2026.
points.quote: We believe the target entity has strong potential for value creation, and it also aligns with our objective of portfolio diversification.

points.point: A separate insolvency acquisition did not survive: the NCLT rejected AIIL's resolution plan for Vas Infrastructure Limited on July 7, 2026, and AIIL said this changed nothing operationally.
points.quote: We would further like to state that on account of the aforesaid rejection of the resolution plan there is no impact on the business operations of the Company.

points.point: Capital actions in the window are expansionary and promoter/subsidiary-funding oriented, not separation-related: a 4:1 bonus issue of 67,93,80,400 shares out of Rs. 8,880.02 crore of reserves at September 30, 2025, taking paid-up equity from 16,98,45,100 to 84,92,25,500 shares.

verdict.rationale: The texts provided do not describe a separation, spin-off or demerger at all, and no earnings-call passages were supplied — the CALL PASSAGES section is empty, so nothing can be attributed to management commentary. What the filing text describes is the opposite transaction: a Scheme of Amalgamation in which Cigniti Technologies Limited (the Transferor Company, a digital assurance and engineering / software-testing business using AI-driven Continuous Testing and Test Automation, listed on BSE and NSE) is merged into Coforge Limited (the Transferee Company, an IT and IT-enabled services provider across financial services, insurance, travel, transportation and logistics, manufacturing and distribution, and government). The commercial backdrop given is that Coforge had already bought control before the scheme: by 27 December 2024 it held 54% of Cigniti's expanded share capital, having acquired 72,35,865 equity shares between October and December 2024 for approximately INR 10,239 million, and both boards approved the original scheme that same day, 27 December 2024. Consideration was set by a Joint Valuation Report of PwC Business Consulting Services LLP and KPMG Valuation Services LLP at a share exchange ratio of 1:5 (one INR 10 Coforge share for five INR 10 Cigniti shares), with fairness opinions from JM Financial Limited and Axis Capital Limited. That ratio was later restated to 1:1 by a Joint Clarification Note dated 13 June 2025 purely because Coforge split each INR 10 share into five INR 2 shares (board 04 March 2025, shareholders 17 April 2025, record date 04 June 2025); the filing stresses the revised ratio is "mathematically and economically equivalent" to the original and conveys no substantive change in value, with Axis (16 June 2025) and JM Financial (19 June 2025) reconfirming fairness, and both boards approving the amended scheme on 06 July 2025. Critically, the extract itself does not reproduce the rationale: it states the rationale "ha[s] been set out in detail in the First Motion Order dated 17 October 2025" and is only "briefly recapitulated herein", and the recapitulation that follows is procedural — incorporation history, registered-office shifts to Gurugram, share capital, exchange ratio, exchange and tribunal steps — with no stated synergy, margin, capital, focus or valuation reasoning. No investor, lender or partner is identified as having asked for the transaction; stakeholders simply voted in favour, and no objections were received from any shareholder or creditor.
verdict.evolution: No earnings calls were provided, so there is no call-by-call evolution and no call dates to cite. The only sequence available is from the filing: board approval of the original scheme plus the 1:5 valuation and fairness opinions on 27 December 2024, after Coforge's October–December 2024 purchase of 54% of Cigniti; the Coforge stock split (board 04 March 2025, shareholders 17 April 2025, record date 04 June 2025) prompting the 13 June 2025 restatement of the ratio to 1:1 and amended board approvals on 06 July 2025; then NSE and BSE observation letters on 17 and 18 July 2025, the First Motion Order of 17 October 2025, stakeholder meetings on 06 December 2025, Chairperson's Reports of 08 December 2025, the Second Motion petition filed 15 December 2025, and admission by the Tribunal on 09 January 2026. That is a change in transaction mechanics and process, not a change in a separation plan.

verdict.what_management_expects: Nothing is stated. The supplied texts contain no management expectations for margins, capital allocation, valuation or business focus, and no post-transaction operating or financial targets for either entity. verdict.rationale: On the texts supplied there is no separation, demerger, spin-off or carve-out of any Happiest Minds business: the only corporate event is the opposite — Happiest Minds Technologies is being dissolved into ITC Infotech India Limited by merger by absorption, alongside a partial exit by its promoter, so the honest reading for a special-situation investor is a combination plus a de-promoterisation, not a separation. The Board approved on August 31, 2026 a Scheme of Amalgamation under Sections 230–232 whereby Happiest Minds (the Transferor) merges into ITC Infotech (the Transferee), Happiest Minds shareholders receive 25 ITC Infotech shares of ₹10 for every 81 Happiest Minds shares of ₹2, ITC Infotech's shares then list on BSE/NSE, and 'the Transferor Company shall be dissolved without being wound up'; in parallel Ashok Soota and Ashok Soota Medical Research LLP sell 22.106% of the company (3,36,61,700 shares) to ITC Infotech for ₹1,329.72 crore in two tranches at ₹390 and ₹400 (average ~₹395, against an assessed ₹405), leaving ITC Limited with ~73.4% and public holders ~26.6%, of which Soota keeps ~7.55% as the largest individual shareholder but explicitly 'will not be a promoter.' The separation that management did explain is therefore the promoter's separation from the company: Venkatraman said Soota had 'expressed his intention to pare down his stake in the Company to fund his legacy not-for-profit organizations, SKAN, and also to capitalize his healthcare venture Happiest Health,' and that 'the funding needs of these entities have since then grown substantially' — an escalation from the Aug 13, 2024 call, where Soota said the same purposes but promised not to go below 40% and expected no further sale 'in the next two to four years.' The business case given for the merger is scale and complementarity, not focus through separation: combined FY26 revenue of ₹7,033 crore (Happiest Minds ₹2,315 crore + ITC Infotech ₹4,718 crore), 19,000+ people, 800+ customers, 30+ countries, India's 11th largest listed IT services player, 9,000+ AI-trained professionals, and a geographic mix of ~38% Americas / ~31% Europe / ~31% rest of world versus Happiest Minds' 59% Americas and 8% Europe. Management said the explicit problem it solves is the stranded US$1 billion revenue ambition: Venkatraman admitted 'our goal of our possibility of reaching that goal looked difficult earlier, now but it is very well within sight,' with the target pulled from FY31 to FY28; Joseph framed the industry problem as AI-led spending, outcome focus and accelerating vendor consolidation requiring 'broader capabilities and greater execution scale,' with Happiest Minds strong in AI, digital, product engineering, cloud, data and cybersecurity and ITC Infotech in enterprise transformation, SAP, PLM, Industry 4.0 and industry solutions, almost no overlap in top customers, and a partner ecosystem (Microsoft, SAP, ServiceNow, PTC, Google, Amazon) where a ₹7,000-crore entity matters more. Valuation was set by PwC and Grant Thornton with an ICICI Securities fairness opinion at 15.1x FY26 EBITDA for Happiest Minds versus 13.6x for ITC Infotech — 'reflecting the relative premium that has been attributed to Happiest Minds' — implying ₹6,167 crore for Happiest Minds, ~₹11,920 crore for ITC Infotech and ₹18,087 crore combined. Nobody is recorded as demanding this: no investor, lender or partner asked for a separation; the only pressures visible in the calls are retail shareholder anger at the stock ('we are not happy indeed. So please do something... I request to improve your balance sheet,' Feb 10, 2026) and the promoter's own funding need, while lenders appear only mechanically — the outstanding NCDs are to be redeemed by September 26, 2026 so that 'no new NCDs will be issued pursuant to the Scheme,' and no open offer is triggered because the purchase stops at 22.1%, below the 25% threshold. The earlier, far smaller 'separation' threads in the calls were internal, not structural: a separate P&L planned for the Arttha banking product/SaaS business (May 13, 2025), a standalone Generative AI business unit with its own P&L, CEO and COO, and Happiest Health kept outside the listed company with an IPO Soota said 'could be easily 6 years away' — while the actual legal activity in the period ran toward consolidation, with PureSoftware and Aureustech amalgamated into Happiest Minds (NCLT orders received June 5 and August 18, 2026, appointed date April 1, 2026).
verdict.evolution: The idea first surfaced only as promoter liquidity: on the Aug 13, 2024 call Soota explained a bulk sale to fund SKAN and Happiest Health, capped himself at 40% and expected no further sale for two to four years; on May 13, 2025 and Jul 30, 2025 the $1bn-by-FY31 vision was openly questioned and management said it would 'restate where we stand on that goal,' while separation talk was limited to a separate P&L for Arttha and the standalone GenAI BU. On Feb 10, 2026 an investor put press reports of a Soota stake sale directly to him and he denied any change ('Make no mistake, I am here to completely see it through'), promising instead 'a new trajectory' and a 'secret weapon' (AI First, Agile Always) at Q4; on May 29, 2026 and Jul 28, 2026 management still guided standalone FY27 revenue growth of 12.5% with a 15% FY28 aspiration and said nothing about a transaction. The plan then changed completely on Aug 31, 2026, when the Board approved the Scheme of Amalgamation, the Merger Framework Agreement, the 22.106% promoter share purchase agreement at ₹390/₹400 and even a shift of the registered office from Karnataka to West Bengal, explained on the Sep 1, 2026 special-purpose call; by the Nov 2, 2026 Q2 FY27 release the merger was 'progressing well and remains on track,' with ₹398 lakh of merger costs booked as an exceptional item and the FY28 US$1 billion aspiration restated.
