verdict.rationale: Across these texts BELRISE never announced a spin-off, demerger or hive-off of any business; the only separation ever discussed is the non-manufacturing commodity trading business, and it remains an unresolved idea rather than a plan. Management describes that business as trading in commodities — high-tensile steel, different grades of coils, metals and alloys, and lithium-ion batteries — and it shows up in consolidated accounts only as 'Purchase of Stock-in-trade' (INR 3,428.96m in Q4 FY26, INR 16,217.43m in FY26), i.e. it sits outside the manufacturing P&L. It is large: roughly INR 430 crore of revenue in Q1 FY26 at about 19% of consolidated revenue (about 20% the prior year), about INR 920 crore in H1 FY26 growing 5-6%, and an implied INR ~17,745m for FY26 (total revenue INR 95,091m less manufacturing revenue INR 77,346m). The stated problem is margin dilution and nothing else: trading runs at about a 6% EBITDA margin against manufacturing EBITDA margins of 13.8-14.3%, which is why consolidated EBITDA margin (12.1% in FY26) sits well below manufacturing EBITDA margin (13.7%) — an analyst put it directly as 'on a consolidated basis it is margin dilutive.' Management's counter-argument for keeping it is informational, not financial: the commodity trading book gives them 'deeper insights into global raw material indices,' which supports their back-to-back raw-material pricing model with customers. The pressure to separate came entirely from sell-side analysts — Saurabh Jain (Sunidhi Securities) asked for help valuing it and for 'plans to hive off this business as discussed earlier' on 12 Nov 2025, and Vipul Agrawal (HSBC) raised 'a spin off of the whole entity' on the 25 May 2026 call; no lenders, JV partners or customers are cited anywhere as requesting it. Management's position actually hardened against it over the year: 'still evaluating' a hive-off in November 2025, then 'we have not commented on hiving off this business in any format' in May 2026, with no board approval, valuation, registered valuer, fairness opinion or scheme ever filed for a separation. Every corporate action that was actually approved runs the other way — consolidating entities into the listed company (H-One India merger approved 11 Nov 2025 and refiled to NCLT Mumbai; Badve Autocomps and Eximius Infra Tech merger approved 31 Jan 2026, exchange observation letters 3 July 2026; plus the Hyva India tipper-body slump-sale purchase on 4 Aug 2026).
verdict.evolution: The trading business is first quantified on the 12 Aug 2025 Q1 FY26 call (INR 430 crore, ~6% EBITDA margin, ~19% of consolidated revenue), where the hive-off is already referred to as previously discussed, implying it surfaced on the omitted earlier call. On 12 Nov 2025 (Q2 FY26) it becomes explicit: an investor asks for help valuing it and for hive-off plans, and management says it is 'still evaluating' the option while defending the business as a window into global raw-material indices. The 2 Feb 2026 (Q3 FY26) call drops the topic entirely and instead presents the opposite structural move — absorbing two promoter entities to cut related-party transactions by ~INR 11.5bn. By the 25 May 2026 Q4/FY26 call (tagged Jun 2026) the idea has gone backwards: management states it has not commented on hiving off the business in any format and offers only to keep investors updated.

points.point: First quantification of the business later floated for separation: commodity trading of high-tensile steel, coil grades and lithium-ion batteries, ~INR 430 crore in Q1 FY26, ~19% of consolidated revenue (vs ~20% in FY25), at roughly a 6% EBITDA margin versus manufacturing EBITDA margin of 13.8%.
points.quote: And the trading margins that we have are of course, lower than manufacturing business, close to a 6% EBITDA margin.

points.point: An investor (Saurabh Jain, Sunidhi Securities) explicitly asks management to help value the trading business and to update on hive-off plans, flagging it as weighing on H1 FY26 profitability at ~INR 920 crore of revenue.
points.quote: Something, which can help us to value this business and your plans to hive off this business as discussed earlier?

points.point: Management's only on-record openness to separating it: the hive-off is under evaluation but not committed, with H1 trading revenue growth of 5-6% and EBITDA margin still near 6% versus manufacturing EBITDA margin of 14.2%.
points.quote: In terms of your question of hiving off, while we have not commented on that publicly, we are still evaluating if that would be a potential option that we could consider.

points.point: The stated reason for retaining the business is informational rather than financial — the trading book feeds visibility on raw-material indices, which underpins the back-to-back steel/plastic pricing pass-through management later says protects gross margins.
points.quote: The perspective is that by using this commodity trading business, we are able to get deeper insights into global raw material indices.

points.point: Instead of separating anything, the board approves absorbing two promoter-owned entities (Badve Autocomps, FY25 revenue ~INR 14bn, PAT INR 793m; Eximius Infra Tech, ~INR 7bn, PAT INR 330m) at 8.3x P/E versus Belrise at ~30.9x, to simplify the group and strip out related-party transactions.
points.quote: Firstly, the merger will result in a significantly simplified group structure, with related-party transactions reducing materially by close to INR11.5 billion.

points.point: Vipul Agrawal (HSBC) revives the idea, attributing an earlier reference to the Managing Director and framing the rationale purely as consolidated margin dilution (FY26 consolidated EBITDA margin 12.1% versus manufacturing 13.7%).
points.quote: Earlier, Shrikant sir talked about like maybe you might localize some products in India or maybe a spin off of the whole entity because again it's on a consolidated basis it is margin dilutive.

points.point: Management walks the idea back to zero, declining any commitment on separating the trading business and offering no timeline, structure, valuation or expected benefit.
points.quote: Yes, we have not commented on hiving off this business in any format.

points.point: No scheme of arrangement for a separation exists in the filings; both schemes are mergers into the listed entity (H-One India approved 11 Nov 2025 and refiled to NCLT Mumbai after withdrawal from NCLT Allahabad; Badve Autocomps and Eximius approved 31 Jan 2026, with NSE/BSE 'no adverse observations' letters dated 3 July 2026), and the only August 2026 transaction is an inbound slump-sale purchase of Hyva India's tipper-body business for ~USD 5.65m.
points.quote: Considered and approved scheme of Amalgamation amongst Badve Autocomps Private Limited, Eximius Infra Tech Solutions Private Limited (Transferor Company) and Belrise Industries Limited (Transferee Company) and their respective shareholders and creditors.

verdict.what_management_expects: Management states no expected benefit — no margin, capital, valuation or focus claim is ever made for separating the trading business, and no standalone entity is described. The accretion case is the analysts': removing a ~6%-margin, ~19%-of-revenue book would lift consolidated margins toward manufacturing's 13.7%. Management instead claims retention value via raw-material-index visibility.
verdict.gaps: No separation structure, valuation, timing, debt or asset split, standalone trading financials or balance sheet, counterparty list, board view, or why evaluation stalled between November 2025 and May 2026.

verdict.rationale: The business being separated is Awfis Transform, the company's Design & Build (D&B) / construction-and-fit-out vertical, which is being hived off from Awfis Space Solutions Ltd. into Awfis Transform Private Limited (ATPL, incorporated 03 December 2025), a wholly owned subsidiary, by way of a slump sale on a going-concern basis under a Business Transfer Agreement dated 23 December 2025 for an Initial Purchase Price of INR 265.91 million (valuation under Section 50B / Rule 11UAE, reference date 30 September 2025, valuer Gaurav Sukhija of Kirtane & Pandit LLP), with the final price to be reset on an updated valuation as at closing per the 24 March 2026 addendum. Management's stated reasoning on the Nov 2025 call was that D&B is a 'high potential' growth engine that deserves separate tracking for 'greater focus, strategic clarity and scalability', and that a separate entity gives it 'enhanced flexibility in capital deployment, strategic partnerships and expansion initiatives', plus a dedicated leadership team — explicitly so it can move beyond commercial workplace interiors into retail, hospitality and institutional projects, where Amit Ramani conceded the expertise 'will have to be built either organically or inorganically'. The second, investor-driven reason was cost transparency: Ramani said a recurring piece of feedback was 'can we split these costs properly', so the two businesses can be tracked on a stand-alone basis; the Feb 2026 call confirmed subsidiarisation is what unlocks the leadership bandwidth to chase the new sectors (D&B was then still ~95% commercial workplace interiors). The scale and economics make the split material: D&B contributed INR 2,782.58 million, 23.13% of FY25 turnover, and INR 712.67 million / 15.60% of net worth, but earns only ~7–8% net margins (7.5% PBT) versus 36.8% operating EBITDA margins in coworking, and it is a fixed-cost business whose FY26 revenue fell on GRAP-IV pollution curbs, project deferrals and fewer managed-aggregation deals while third-party work grew from INR 95 crore (FY25) to INR 152 crore (FY26), lifting third-party share from 47% to 59%. The filings' own rationale is 'enhanced operational efficiency, business synergies, and a more focused and specialized management structure, as a part of corporate strategy', with the undertaking transferred with all assets, licences, employees, liabilities and litigations on an 'as is where is' basis. No lender or partner is cited as asking for it; shareholder approval was required only because the undertaking generates over 20% of total income (Section 180(1)(a)) and was obtained by postal ballot on 22/23 January 2026 with 99.9975% of votes in favour (4,70,49,179 for, 1,177 against). Management stresses there is no change in economic interest because ATPL is a wholly owned, consolidated subsidiary and shareholders remain the ultimate beneficiaries, and the transaction is outside any Scheme of Arrangement and exempt from Regulation 37A and Section 188 approval. Notably the furniture vertical, Frame by Awfis, was deliberately kept in the core entity rather than moved into the D&B entity.
verdict.evolution: The idea surfaced as framing before structure: on the May 26, 2025 call Sumit Lakhani described D&B as 'a full-fledged separate vertical, which has become large', and on November 11, 2025 the Q2 FY26 call announced the 'planned subsidiarization of Awfis Transform' on the same day the Board authorised an in-principle slump sale to a wholly owned subsidiary then still under incorporation. It hardened fast: ATPL was incorporated 03 December 2025, the BTA was executed 23 December 2025 at INR 265.91 million with completion promised 'on or before 28 February 2026', and shareholders approved it by postal ballot concluding 22 January 2026 (result 23 January 2026). Then it slipped twice — on 26 February 2026 the Board pushed completion to end-CY2026 citing procedural, administrative, operational and transition-related requirements, an addendum on 24 March 2026 moved final pricing to a closing-date valuation, and on 03 November 2026 the Board deferred it beyond CY2026 with no fixed date, management now expecting completion 'in the next twelve months' while D&B is reported as a discontinued operation under Ind AS 105. The Feb 2026 call reaffirmed the purpose (leadership freedom to enter new sectors), while the May 25, 2026 call discussed Transform at length as a 'stand-alone business' yet never mentioned the pending transfer at all.

points.point: First signal of separate treatment: Lakhani frames Design & Build as a distinct, now-large vertical inside the company, growing ~20-25% industry CAGR, with Awfis targeting larger mandates.
points.quote: So primarily, the way we look internally in our business is Design & Build is a full-fledged separate vertical, which has become large.

points.point: Formal announcement of the planned subsidiarisation of Awfis Transform, justified as separate tracking for focus, clarity and scalability of a vertical management calls a key growth engine.
points.quote: We believe this vertical represents a key growth engine for Awfis and tracking it separately will enable greater focus, strategic clarity and scalability.

points.point: The structural purpose: a separate entity is meant to give D&B its own capital deployment, partnerships and expansion capacity, plus dedicated leadership and freed-up management bandwidth at the parent.
points.quote: This move is designed to optimize management bandwidth and unlock new growth opportunities by providing entity with the enhanced flexibility in capital deployment, strategic partnerships and expansion initiatives to scale the business.

points.point: Stated end-market reason: D&B is to expand beyond workplace interiors into retail, hospitality and institutional projects, with a dedicated leadership team and its own financial visibility.
points.quote: The business now aims to expand beyond workplace design and build into new segments such as retail, hospitality and institutional projects, supported by a dedicated leadership team and a clear financial visibility.

points.point: Who asked for it: answering Girish Choudhary (Avendus Spark) on capital allocation, leadership bandwidth and overhead sharing, Ramani cited persistent investor feedback demanding a clean cost split so each business can be tracked stand-alone.
points.quote: And again, when you look at the co-working business and our Transform business, one of the feedbacks that we have always gotten is that can we split these costs properly.

points.point: Admission that the new sectors require capability Awfis does not yet have, implying the subsidiary may need to buy it — a reason for an entity with its own capital and partnership flexibility.
points.quote: On retail and hospitality, some of that expertise will have to be built either organically or inorganically going forward.

points.point: Scope limit on the separation: the nascent furniture vertical (later Frame by Awfis, run via 5+ contract manufacturers) is deliberately retained in the parent rather than placed in the D&B entity.
points.quote: So currently, the plan is to keep it as part of the core entity as well, not move into the D&B entity.

points.point: Subsidiarisation is explicitly the enabler of diversification, not an immediate pivot: D&B was still ~95% commercial workplace interiors, with the entire ~8-9 lakh sq ft third-party pipeline (~INR 200 crore) from commercial workplaces.
points.quote: The plan was not to immediately go into these new segments, but as we subsidiarize this business, the idea was that this would give the leadership of that business the opportunity to expand into those avenues.

points.point: Although the pending transfer went unmentioned on this call, management described Transform as already operating as a stand-alone business, with third-party revenue up from INR 95 crore to INR 152 crore and third-party share from 47% to 59%.
points.quote: This is no longer a support function. It's just a stand-alone business with its own client relationships, its own capability stack and its own compounding pipeline.

points.point: The filings' own rationale for the slump sale of D&B (23.13% of FY25 turnover, INR 2,782.58 million; 15.60% of net worth, INR 712.67 million) to wholly owned subsidiary ATPL at an initial consideration of INR 265.91 million.
points.quote: In order to achieve enhanced operational efficiency, business synergies, and a more focused and specialized management structure, as a part of corporate strategy, it is proposed to sell, transfer or otherwise dispose of D&B Business to its wholly owned subsidiary, Awfis Transform Private Limited by way of a slump sale on a going concern basis

points.point: Shareholder approval was needed only under Section 180(1)(a) because the undertaking generates over 20% of total income; the postal ballot closing 22 January 2026 passed with 4,70,49,179 votes for and 1,177 against (99.9975%).
points.quote: Since the proposed transaction involves transfer of the Undertaking, which generated more than 20% of the total income of the Company during the previous financial year, approval of the shareholders under Section 180 (1) (a) of the Act and all other applicable laws is being sought.

points.point: Management insists the split is structural, not economic: because ATPL is a consolidated wholly owned subsidiary, shareholders remain the ultimate beneficiaries and group financials are unaffected.
points.quote: The sale of the said Undertaking will not have any impact on the Company's existing business or on the economic interest of the shareholders since the proposed transaction is with a wholly-owned subsidiary Company and the members will remain the ultimate beneficiary.

points.point: Completion slipped from 28 February 2026 to end-CY2026 (26 February 2026 board) and then indefinitely on 03 November 2026, with D&B meanwhile classified as a discontinued operation under Ind AS 105 (H1 FY27 income INR 1,485.39 million, PBT INR 109.15 million).
points.quote: The deferral is necessitated by procedural, administrative, operational and transition-related requirements that need to be addressed before completion of the transaction.

verdict.what_management_expects: Awfis Transform: dedicated leadership, own capital deployment, partnerships and organic/inorganic entry into retail, hospitality and institutional work, scaling toward a full-service D&B platform. Parent: freed management bandwidth, cleanly split costs, sharper premium-flex/GCC focus. Investors: stand-alone tracking of both P&Ls. Economic interest unchanged, since ATPL is wholly owned and consolidated.
verdict.gaps: No explanation of INR 265.91mn price versus INR 712.67mn net worth, tax effects, outside capital or eventual listing, margin targets, or the repeated timeline slippage.

verdict.rationale: The business being separated is Bikaji's frozen-and-bakery arm, housed in Bikaji Bakes Private Limited (BBPL), which went from a 100% wholly-owned subsidiary to a 70:30 joint venture after Bikaji sold a 30% equity stake to Mr. Thayekunni Khaleel, founder of the Middle East bakery brand 'Bakemart'. Management's stated reason is capability and expertise rather than cash: Khaleel is described as "a big name in Middle East and having more than 4 decades of experience in bakery category", and the Jan 27, 2026 board filing says the Joint Venture cum Shareholders Agreement exists "to synergize the combined experience and expertise efforts of the Parties... for undertaking the frozen and bakery business in India, on a joint venture basis" using the existing BBPL shell in proportion 70:30. The second reason is distance from the core: bakery is deliberately kept out of the Bikaji namkeen/sweets organisation — "it will be a complete separate team, not that anything to do with Bikaji. This will be run by a professional team" — and even the brand is ring-fenced ("not Bikaji for sure"), with the JV company owning the brands, trademarks and IP outright per the filing. Third, the business model is one Bikaji's existing sales machine cannot serve: croissants, premium breads, viennoiseries, cakes and pastries, all frozen, sold mainly as air-freight exports, then B2B, with domestic (top-end stores, q-com/e-com) the smallest leg — Khaleel's existing Middle East route-to-market is what makes the export leg work. Scale cited: "over 3 years... this has a potential to get us about INR100 crores in our top line number," against a plant set up in Bangalore that management said in January 2026 would be commissioned "by end of this quarter only." Financially the carve-out is tiny and loss-making at the time of separation: BBPL reported NIL turnover and NIL revenue for FY26, income of ₹319.83 thousand, and negative net worth of ₹(6,128.46) thousand, and Bikaji had earlier funded it with a ₹5 crore loan (July 2025) — the 30% stake changed hands for a consideration of just ₹30,000. No investor, lender or analyst asked for the separation; analysts (Shirish Pardeshi of Motilal Oswal, Anchit of Goldman Sachs) instead challenged the rationale, asking whether the company was diverging into biscuits, what the scalability was, whether Khaleel's UAE stores came with the deal (they did not — "This is Bikaji Bakes. This is Indian stuff only"), and under what brand it would sell. Structurally it fits the "house of brands" approach management described from Oct 2024 onward, where new categories sit in separate entities (THF, Ariba, Bikaji Foods Retail, Bikaji CG Nepal) rather than inside Bikaji Foods.
verdict.evolution: Jul 24, 2025 (Jul 2025 call): Bikaji Bakes surfaces only as a ₹5 crore loan to a 100% subsidiary doing 'some bakery items', mostly e-commerce, and 'currently it's in Bikaji brand' — i.e. wholly owned and Bikaji-branded. Jan 27–28, 2026 (board filing and Feb 2026 call): the plan flips to a 70:30 JV with Bakemart founder Thayekunni Khaleel, with Deepak Agarwal personally a party, a separate professional team, a non-Bikaji brand owned by the JV, a Bangalore plant and a ₹100 crore three-year ambition. May 22, 2026 (May 2026 call): Bikaji Bakes is not mentioned at all, even while THF, Ariba and exports are discussed. Aug 26, 2026 filing: the 30% sale completes for ₹30,000, BBPL ceases to be a wholly-owned subsidiary and continues as a 70%-held subsidiary.

points.point: First disclosure: Bikaji Bakes is a 100%-owned bakery vehicle funded by a ₹5 crore loan from the parent, pitched as a small e-commerce-led investment and, at that stage, still under the Bikaji brand.
points.quote: So, that's number one and number two, from Bikaji Bakes’ lens, it's a 100% subsidiary of Bikaji Foods focusing on doing , focusing on making some bakery items.

points.point: Management framed the bakery entry as a small, opportunistic spend riding the growth of bakery in India, with e-commerce as the route and the Bikaji brand as the initial label.
points.quote: So, that's a small investment what we will do and we will focus on doing crossover and everything, small bakery, bakery investment.

points.point: The separation is announced as a JV in which Bikaji keeps 70% and Khaleel takes 30%, justified by his four decades of Middle East bakery experience — expertise, not capital, is the stated driver.
points.quote: And also, we have done a JV with T. K. Khaleel. T. K. Khaleel is a big name in Middle East and having more than 4 decades of experience in bakery category.

points.point: Structure spelled out: 30% to Khaleel, 70% to Bikaji, housed in Bikaji Bakes as a separate company under Bikaji rather than inside the listed operating business.
points.quote: He has made some big business in bakery in Middle East, and we have tied up with him and formed a JV where he will be having 30% stake, and we will be having 70% stake in our company in Bikaji Bakes, a separate company under Bikaji.

points.point: Shirish Pardeshi (Motilal Oswal) pressed management on why the company was diverging into bakery at all and on the scalability of the model — the challenge came from analysts, not a demand for separation.
points.quote: Okay. Just last question on BBPL. What is the rationale?

points.point: The operating logic of separation: three product segments (premium breads, grocery, cakes), three channels led by frozen air-freight exports then B2B then a small domestic leg — a model distinct from Bikaji's namkeen distribution.
points.quote: So, this would have 3 parts of it. So very premium breads, grocery and then the third is cakes.

points.point: Explicit organisational ring-fencing: a wholly separate professional team with no overlap with the Bikaji business, which is the clearest statement of why the business is being held outside the core.
points.quote: So, this will not be , it will be a complete separate team, not that anything to do with Bikaji.

points.point: Brand separation confirmed in answer to Anchit (Goldman Sachs): the bakery business will not carry the Bikaji name, to be announced before the Bangalore factory is commissioned.
points.quote: We'll announce it shortly before we commission the factory, but not Bikaji for sure.

points.point: Size of the prize and the capex position: a futuristic investment with a ₹100 crore top-line potential over three years, revenue starting from year one, plant in Bangalore live by end of Q4 FY26.
points.quote: And as Rishabh said, that over 3 years, I mean, this has a potential to get us about INR100 crores in our top line number.

points.point: Khaleel's existing Middle East retail operations are explicitly excluded from the deal — the JV is India-manufactured product for export, not an acquisition of his stores.
points.quote: No, no. So, this is Bikaji Bakes . This is Indian stuff only.

points.point: The Jan 27, 2026 board approval states the purpose of the JV cum Shareholders Agreement among BFIL, Deepak Agarwal and Khaleel: pooling combined experience and expertise for the frozen and bakery business in India at 70:30, using the existing BBPL shell.
points.quote: BFIL, Mr. Deepak and Mr. Khaleel (collectively, referred as the “Parties ”) entered into a Joint Venture cum Shareholders Agreement (“Agreement ”) to synergize the combined experience and expertise efforts of the Parties to the Agreement for undertaking the frozen and bakery business in India, on a joint venture basis, by utiliz ing an existing Company i.e. Bikaji Bakes Private Limited (“JV Company ” or “BBPL ”), in proportion of 70:30.

points.point: The whole frozen bakery value chain, including brands, trademarks and IP, is moved into the JV entity rather than retained by the listed parent — consistent with the 'not Bikaji' branding decision.
points.quote: The JV Company will manufacture, trade, retail, wholesale, manage and operate the entire frozen bakery and allied business, including brands, trademarks and Intellectual Property(ies) , thus,  enabling the Parties to achieve their shared business objectives through collaborative efforts.

points.point: Governance is shared, not merely economic: directors are nominated in proportion to shareholding and significant matters — new securities, borrowings, acquisitions, investments, mergers, winding-up, auditors — need unanimous consent, so Bikaji gives up unilateral control despite holding 70%.
points.quote: Significant Decision Matters of JV Company : - Unanimous consent of the Parties  will be required for  the significant matters , such as , issue of new securities, borrowings,  acquisitions, investments, amalgamation and merger,  winding -up, change in auditors, etc.

points.point: Completion on Aug 26, 2026: the 30% stake is sold to Khaleel and BBPL ceases to be a wholly-owned subsidiary while Bikaji retains 70% and consolidates it as a subsidiary.
points.quote: Consequential to aforesaid sale of the Company’s  equity stake, BBPL  has ceased to be WOS  of the Company . The Company continues to hold remaining 7 0% equity stake in BBPL  and accordingly, it will remain a Subsidiary of the Company .

points.point: The separated business was pre-revenue and loss-making at the point of separation — NIL turnover and revenue in FY26, income of ₹319.83 thousand and negative net worth of ₹61.28 lakh — and the 30% stake changed hands for only ₹30,000 on an arm's-length, related-party basis (Deepak and Shweta Agarwal are BBPL directors).
points.quote:
Turnover - NIL 
Revenue - NIL 
Income - ₹ 319.83 (in Thousand)  
Net Worth - ₹ (6,128.46)  (in Thousand)

points.point: No mention of Bikaji Bakes, the JV or the Bangalore bakery plant anywhere in the Q4 FY26 call, even while THF, Ariba, exports, the Nepal JV and capex plans were discussed in detail.
points.quote: So, capex largely what we'll be doing, there's 2 capex, the sweet factory, which is coming in Bikaner.

verdict.what_management_expects: For the JV: a professionally run, separately branded frozen-bakery business — croissants, premium breads, viennoiseries, cakes — reaching roughly ₹100 crore top line in three years, revenue from year one, led by air-freight exports on Khaleel's Middle East route-to-market, then B2B, then premium domestic and q-com. For Bikaji: a futuristic adjacency gained without diluting management focus, capital or brand in its core ethnic-snacks business.
verdict.gaps: No stated valuation basis for the ₹30,000 price, Khaleel's capital commitment, margin or EBITDA impact, why FY26 revenue was nil, or any post-JV progress update.

verdict.rationale: The business actually being separated is the Portfolio Management Services (PMS) business of IIFL Capital Services Ltd, which was hived off to IIFL Capital Asset Management Limited (ICAML), a wholly owned subsidiary, by way of a slump sale on a going concern basis under a Business Transfer Agreement — first intimated on July 28, 2025, executed with SEBI approval as disclosed on December 30, 2025, and completed when SEBI cancelled the parent's Portfolio Manager registration No. INP000002213 with effect from May 20, 2026. The only rationale management ever put in writing is the Regulation 30 disclosure: the move is 'part of a broader commercial strategy to align business verticals for operational efficiency, simplify regulatory structures, and leverage growth opportunities', and it is 'expected to enhance operational efficiency and help focused growth of the PMS business under the wholly owned subsidiary'. The filings stress it is a parent-to-WOS transaction ('undertaken between the holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary'), outside any Scheme of Arrangement, with 'Nil' change in shareholding pattern and no benefit to the promoter/promoter group — i.e. framed as licence and entity housekeeping, not value unlocking. No investor, lender or partner is named as having asked for it; the trigger implied by the filings is regulatory architecture, since ICAML separately holds Investment Adviser, Portfolio Manager and AIF registrations whose change of control then had to be cleared as a condition precedent for Fairfax's move to 51%. On the earnings calls the carve-out is never mentioned once; the adjacent story management told was building in-house 'manufacturing' — 'we have started AIF, we have started PMS, we have one credit fund, we have one late-stage fund' (July 24, 2026), ₹4,400 crores of AIF/PMS AUM whose income is booked under financial product distribution, a ₹500 crore credit opportunities fund closed in FY26, and asset-management AUM of ₹800–900 crores in April 2025 expected to 'easily double in the next one year' — all while insisting the house stays open-architecture. The separation sits inside a wider simplification: strike-off of the dormant IIFL Securities Services IFSC Limited (nil revenue, negative net worth of ₹2.09 lakh) and transfer of India Infoline Foundation to IIFL Finance for ₹10,000 (September 11, 2026), plus a proposed new wholly owned NBFC subsidiary for HNI/UHNI lending (October 28, 2026). The economic context management did give is the legacy retail broking-to-wealth transformation: wealth was loss-making at ₹20–24 crores in FY25 and another ₹20–25 crores in H1FY26, non-institutional cost-to-income around 75%, with break-even promised 'by next year'.
verdict.evolution: The only separation ever discussed on a call was the older 5Paisa arrangement: on January 23, 2024 management explained SEBI had required a refiling and the Board sent the scheme for transferring online retail customers back 'to the drawing board' to revalue it. The PMS carve-out surfaced only in filings — intimated July 28, 2025, one day before the July 29, 2025 Q1FY26 call where management instead described building AIF/PMS 'manufacturing' and never mentioned the transfer; the BTA and SEBI approval were disclosed December 30, 2025, and the parent's Portfolio Manager registration was cancelled effective May 20, 2026 (disclosed May 22, 2026). Through the February 11, 2026, May 5, 2026 and July 24, 2026 calls the asset-management build-out (₹500 crore credit fund, ₹4,400 crore AIF/PMS AUM) was discussed as growth, with no reference to it now sitting in a separate licensed entity. By the May 7, 2026 Fairfax documents and the October 28, 2026 press release, ICAML's separate change-of-control approvals had become a condition precedent to Fairfax taking 51%, and further pruning followed on September 11, 2026 (IFSC subsidiary strike-off, Foundation transfer).

verdict.rationale: The texts describe two separate things that both fall under 'separation', and neither is a classic demerger of a listed business into a new listed entity. First, Nestlé India carved out businesses by slump sale: the Nutraceutical Business was transferred to Dr. Reddy's and Nestlé Health Science Limited — a 49:51 joint venture (Nestlé India 49%, Dr. Reddy's 51%) that 'came together only in July of last year' (July 2024) — and the Nestlé Business Services Division was transferred to Nestlé Business Services India Private Limited (formerly Purina PetCare India Private Limited), a Nestlé affiliate; the gains on both appear as exceptional items of Rs 2,908.2 million standalone and Rs 1,834.2 million consolidated for the nine months to 31 December 2024 and FY ended 31 March 2025. The only rationale management gave, in the 4 February 2025 analyst meet, was capability complementarity rather than any problem with the parent: Nestlé India is 'a consumer product company with a more limited health care exposure as compared to Dr. Reddy's which is a health care company', so the JV 'combin[es] the synergies of product portfolio and distribution reach' to attack an addressable health-science/nutrition opportunity management sized at 'INR 24,000 Crores', with Nestlé Health Science products to be 'by and large manufactured locally' using Nestlé's R&D base (INR 1.8 billion R&D spend in CY2023, 4,000+ employees, 23 sites). Suresh Narayanan reported the integration as 'successful', the teams 'working well together', 'double digit growth', and new launches on the anvil from both the Nestlé Health Science and Dr. Reddy's portfolios; he sits on the JV board. Second, and legally distinct, a Scheme of Arrangement sanctioned by the NCLT New Delhi Bench on 15 September 2023 and effective 19 October 2023 reclassified Rs 8,374.3 million from General Reserve to Retained Earnings — a balance-sheet/distributable-reserve action, out of which Rs 964.2 million was capitalised for the 1:1 bonus issue in August 2025 and the residual Rs 7,410.1 million funds the Rs 2 per share Special Dividend 2026 (Rs 3,856.6 million). Post-separation, the JV is accounted for as an associate, not consolidated, and Nestlé India's consolidated accounts carry a charge for its share of the associate's result (Rs 164.4 million in Q1 FY2026-27, Rs 423.1 million for 9M FY2025-26 and Rs 455.2 million for FY2025-26), so the carved-out business is currently a drag on consolidated versus standalone earnings. Nowhere in these texts did management cite investor, lender or regulatory pressure as the reason; no analyst on the 4 February 2025 call asked a single question about the slump sales or the Scheme.
verdict.evolution: Only one earnings call falls in the window, and the separation was already largely done by then: the Scheme of Arrangement was sanctioned on 15 September 2023 and became effective 19 October 2023, and the Dr. Reddy's JV 'came together only in July of last year', i.e. July 2024, with the slump-sale gains booked in the nine months to 31 December 2024 and FY ended 31 March 2025. At the 4 February 2025 analyst and institutional investors meet, Narayanan presented the JV twice — once as a 'rising health consciousness' growth platform with an INR 24,000 crore opportunity and once under 'Partnerships' as 'the first of its kind in India for Nestlé' — reporting successful integration and double-digit growth, but gave no rationale for the Scheme itself and no financials for the transferred businesses. In every filing after that (30 January 2026 results, 3 July 2026 dividend intimation, 22 July 2026 Q1 results) the Scheme appears only mechanically, as the source of the reclassified Rs 8,374.3 million used for the August 2025 1:1 bonus and the Rs 2 per share Special Dividend 2026; the only new structural step disclosed is the 30 January 2026 in-principle approval of 26% stakes in two captive renewable SPVs with Adani Green Energy and Radiance Renewables, which is not a business separation.

points.point: The slump sales are identified as exceptional items for 9M to 31 December 2024 and FY ended 31 March 2025: the Nutraceutical Business went to the Dr. Reddy's JV and the Nestlé Business Services Division to a Nestlé affiliate (formerly Purina PetCare India Private Limited); gains were Rs 2,908.2 million standalone and Rs 1,834.2 million consolidated.
points.quote: Exceptional items for the nine months ended 31st December 2024 and financial year ended 31st March 2025 comprise of gain on slump sale of the following businesses: Nutraceutical Business to Dr. Reddy's and Nestlé Health Science Limited. Nestlé Business Services Division to Nestlé Business Services India Private Limited (Formerly known as Purina PetCare India Private Limited ).

points.point: The Scheme of Arrangement, separate from the slump sales, was sanctioned by the NCLT New Delhi Bench on 15 September 2023 and effective 19 October 2023, and its only disclosed effect is the reclassification of Rs 8,374.3 million from General Reserve to Retained Earnings.
points.quote: Pursuant to the Scheme of Arrangement (“Scheme” ) sanctioned by the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi Bench, vide its Order dated  15th September 2023, which became effective from 19th October 2023 ( “NCLT Order ”), an amount of Rs. 8,374.3 million was reclassified from General Reserve to Retained Earnings ( “Reclassified Amount under the Scheme” ).

points.point: The reclassified reserve has been used for shareholder returns: Rs 964.2 million capitalised for the 1:1 bonus issue in August 2025, leaving Rs 7,410.1 million from which the Rs 2 per share Special Dividend 2026 (Rs 3,856.6 million) is paid on and from 30 July 2026.

The aforesaid Special Dividend 2026 shall be paid out of the balance reclassified amount of R s. 7,410.1 million included  in the Total Retained Earnings of the Company as at 31st March 2026.

verdict.rationale: What is being 'separated' is not a demerger or spin-off: it is a 40% minority dilution of Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited (NAIF), NAM India's wholly owned alternatives (AIF) subsidiary, to DWS Group GmbH & Co. KGaA via a fresh issue of 3,40,000 equity shares (face value INR 10) at INR 21,569 per share for INR 733,34,60,000 (~INR 733.35 crore), after which NAIF 'will cease to be a wholly owned subsidiary' but 'continue to remain as a subsidiary' — so NAM India keeps control and consolidation, and the filing states 'No impact' on management or control of the listed entity. The stated purpose in the Scheme documents is 'to jointly develop and build a leading alternative investment funds franchise in India along with DWS'; management's own explanation on the calls is purely about distribution reach, not about fixing a problem inside the business. Sikka's logic, repeated across three calls, is that NAM India is strong domestically and has 'very strong Japanese access' through parent Nippon Life Insurance, but 'Europe access was lower', and DWS — described by him as 'the largest asset manager of Europe' (EUR 1,085 bn AUM at Dec 31, 2025, ~5,000 employees per the filing) — is the channel to bring European money into India, 'especially the alternate and the infrastructure side.' The collaboration is explicitly wider than the JV: the Nov 13, 2025 board authorisation says NAM India and DWS 'will also work closely in other areas including passive investment products and global distribution,' and Sikka added it will help the mutual fund business on 'capability of international funds, ETFs, and also offshore money.' Scale context given: NAIF's cumulative AIF commitments were INR 95.8 bn (Q1 FY27, +18% YoY), up from INR 74.1 bn at Q4 FY25; NAIF contributed INR 101.96 crore of turnover (4.6%) and INR 102.18 crore of net worth (3.1%) in the last financial year; non-MF products are ~8% of gross revenue and MF was 91% of FY26 revenue; and Parag confirmed the AIF entity is already 'a profitable company. It's a profitable franchise.' The background pressure visible in the calls is the persistent failure of the offshore/international engine to scale — offshore AUM went from INR 172 bn (Sep-2024) to INR 161 bn (Sep-2025) to INR 139 bn (Mar-2026), and Sikka conceded 'we would have expected offshore contribution to be higher… it is a little binary' — so the DWS tie-up reads as the fix for foreign-inflow access rather than for anything in the domestic MF franchise. Nobody — no investor, lender or regulator — is said to have asked for it; the counterparty link is related-party-adjacent only in that promoter Nippon Life Insurance 'presently holds 5.00% stake in DWS,' and DWS had already been listed in Apr 2025 as one of the Nippon Life network entities through which offshore business was being sourced. The deal is conditional on SEBI and CCI approvals plus consent of NAIF's AIF investors, with a 12-month long-stop date, and the SHA gives DWS board and senior-management appointment rights, reserved matters requiring its consent, a put option, exit rights, non-compete, transfer restrictions and lock-in.
verdict.evolution: Through Jul 2024 and Oct 2024 AIF is only flagged as 'an important focus area' with senior hiring and seed capital, and in Apr 2025 DWS appears merely as one of several Nippon Life network entities (with GENKAI, BBLAM, Cathay) through which offshore money already trickles in, while Nov 2025 shows management conceding offshore is 'a small part of our overall business, but the ambition is to grow bigger.' The idea surfaces formally at the Feb 2026 call (Q3 FY26, held Jan 29, 2026), which discloses the Nov 13, 2025 board authorisation of a strategic collaboration with DWS taking 'up to 40%' of NAIF plus cooperation in passives and global distribution — still only a non-binding agreement, with Sikka declining detail beyond 'the idea will be to get more global flow into India.' By the Apr 2026 call it is called a JV and justified as access to overseas money 'especially the alternate and the infrastructure side' plus spillover to the MF business; the Mar 14, 2026 filings then harden it into signed SHA/SSA with a fixed 40%, INR 733.35 crore price and SEBI/CCI conditions. At the Jul 2026 call the stake is confirmed as 40%, approvals are still awaited, the Japan-plus-Europe positioning is sharpened ('one side it will be Europe and one side it will be Japan'), and unit economics are declined as 'too early.'

points.point: Pre-history: DWS is already named as one of the Nippon Life group entities through which NAM India's offshore business is sourced, alongside Japan, Thailand and Taiwan affiliates.
points.quote: Till now, if you see where most of our business that is coming, international business is coming – you can look at slide in the presentation, whether it is coming through DWS, whether it is from the GENKAI which is Japan, BBLAM which is Bangkok Life Asset Management and Cathay, which is Taiwan.

points.point: Context for the deal: the non-MF businesses (AIF subsidiary, offshore subsidiary) are tiny in the mix but are the stated growth ambition; yields on these products range 60–120 bps versus ~36 bps blended MF yield.
points.quote: Currently, it's a small part of our overall business, but the ambition is to grow bigger.

points.point: First disclosure of the separation: the Nov 13, 2025 board authorisation of DWS acquiring up to 40% of the AIF subsidiary via fresh equity, plus a wider collaboration on passives and global distribution.
points.quote: Our Board of Directors at their meeting on November 13, 2025, authorised the Company to enter into a strategic collaboration with DWS Group (a leading European Asset Manager), wherein DWS intends to acquire a minority stake of up to 40% in Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited by subscribing to fresh issuance of equity shares.

points.point: Management's one-line rationale at first disclosure, delivered in the same breath as the admission that offshore inflows have disappointed and are 'binary'.
points.quote: As I mentioned in my speech earlier, our AIF is getting into a JV with DWS. Again, the idea will be to get more global flow into India.

points.point: The problem the tie-up is meant to address: offshore contribution has undershot management's own expectations for years, partly on USD-INR, and is lumpy institutional-mandate driven rather than predictable like SIPs.
points.quote: I have mentioned in past also - clearly we would have expected offshore contribution to be higher. It has taken a little more time; it is a little binary.

points.point: Purpose restated as sourcing overseas capital specifically for alternates and infrastructure, still under a non-binding agreement at that date.
points.quote: The idea is we clearly see an opportunity to get a lot of overseas money and especially the alternate and the infrastructure side.

points.point: The JV is explicitly not ring-fenced to AIF — management expects collateral capability transfer into the mutual fund business (international funds, ETFs, offshore money).
points.quote: Also, as far as the JV is concerned, it will also help in collaboration not only in the AIF where it will be a JV, but also with the mutual fund business, you know, to as in whether from a capability of international funds, ETFs, and also offshore money.

points.point: The strategic gap being closed is geographic: Japan access was already strong via the parent; Europe was the missing leg.
points.quote: The idea is to keep getting ready as India keeps, you know, getting stronger. More foreign money will come into India and I think building capabilities access, we were always very strong in Japan. So now this JV gives us an access to Europe.

points.point: Management also flags DWS's passive/ETF strength as a reason the partnership could extend to product launches in India if investor demand appears.
points.quote: And to your earlier question, having DWS with us, you know, and DWS is one of the largest international players both in not also in ETF space, but also passives, you know.

points.point: The signed deal (Mar 14, 2026): SHA with the Company, NAIF and DWS plus an SSA, with the stated object of jointly building an India alternatives franchise and DWS taking 40%.
points.quote: To jointly develop and build a leading alternative investment funds franchise in India along with DWS and in pursuance thereof DWS has agreed to acquire a minority stake of 40 percent in NAIF.

points.point: Price and mechanics: INR 733.35 crore of primary capital into NAIF for 3,40,000 fresh shares at INR 21,569 each — money goes into the subsidiary, not to the listed parent as sale proceeds.
points.quote: DWS has agreed to pay a sum of INR 733,34,60,000/- (Indian Rupees Seven Hundred Thirty-Three Crores Thirty-Four Lakhs Sixty Thousand only) as consideration for acquiring 40% equity stake in NAIF by subscribing to 3,40,000 equity shares [having a face value of INR 10/- (Indian Rupees Ten) per share], to be issued by NAIF by way of preferential allotment.

points.point: Scale of what is being diluted: NAIF is ~4.6% of turnover and ~3.1% of net worth — i.e. the separation touches a small slice of the group.
points.quote: During the last financial year, NAIF contributed INR 101.96 crore to the Turnover (4.6%) and INR 102.18 crore to the Net Worth (3.1%) of the Company.

points.point: It is a dilution, not a disposal — NAM India retains consolidation and, per the filing, control of the listed entity is unaffected.
points.quote: After the said issuance of equity shares, NAIF will cease to be a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company and it would continue to remain as a subsidiary.

points.point: Governance price of the deal: DWS gets board and senior-management appointment rights, veto matters, a put option and exit rights, with non-compete, transfer and lock-in restrictions on NAM India.
points.quote: The SHA provides few customarily required covenants which includes inter alia, provisions w.r.t. board composition, senior management appointment, reserved matters requiring DWS's consent, put-option, exit rights granted to DWS, governance related matters, information-sharing obligations, provisions with respect to non-compete, transfer restrictions and lock-in provisions.

points.point: Conditionality and timeline: SEBI and CCI approvals plus consent of NAIF's AIF investors, within a 12-month long-stop date.
points.quote: The proposed transaction is expected to be completed within 12 months from the execution of the Agreement Date ("Long Stop Date") or such other date mutually agreed between the Parties, subject to receipt of regulatory approvals from SEBI and Competition Commission of India and requisite consent of investors of the AIFs managed by NAIF and upon fulfilment of other conditions precedent stipulated in the SSA.

points.point: The counterparty is not formally related, but promoter Nippon Life Insurance already owns 5% of DWS — the plausible origin of the relationship.
points.quote: DWS is not related to the Company in any manner, however, Nippon Life Insurance Company (i.e. the promoter of the Company) presently holds 5.00% stake in DWS.

points.point: Post-signing framing: DWS as Europe's largest asset manager is the whole point of the JV, with approvals still pending.
points.quote: But specifically, and I'd like to touch upon the JV with DWS, we believe from Europe a lot more money can come to India and DWS is the largest asset manager of Europe and the JV has been done with that in mind.

points.point: The competitive-positioning argument: a dual Europe-plus-Japan access channel is claimed as a unique edge for capturing foreign money into India.
points.quote: We have very strong Japanese access. But Europe access was lower -- and we will become one of the unique asset management companies in India where on one side it will be Europe and one side it will be Japan.

points.point: Management refuses to quantify the economics of the deal — no yields, no AUM or revenue contribution.
points.quote: I think it would be too early. We see a very big opportunity there.

points.point: The entity being part-sold is already profitable on its own, and the AIF book stands at INR 95.8 bn of cumulative commitments, up 18% YoY, with fundraising live across listed equity, private credit and direct VC.
points.quote: Yeah, so it's a profitable company. It's a profitable franchise.

verdict.what_management_expects: For NAIF: European capital into Indian alternates and infrastructure, INR 733.35 crore of fresh primary capital inside the subsidiary, DWS board/veto/put rights, and a jointly built 'leading' India AIF franchise that stays a consolidated, already-profitable subsidiary. For NAM India: Europe access added to its Japan access, spillover capability in international funds, ETFs, passives and global distribution. No margin, capital-release or valuation benefit was ever quantified.
verdict.gaps: No margin, valuation, capital-use or AUM targets; why 40%; how the INR 733 cr is deployed; NAIF standalone P&L; put/exit pricing; dilution impact on consolidated EPS; no investor or lender demand cited.

verdict.segment_name: Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited (Nippon India AIF) — not identified as a reportable segment; annual reports state the sole primary segment is asset management services
verdict.measure_notes: No profit line available for the AIF business. Segment notes (AR2024 p.231/285, AR2025 p.246/296, AR2026 p.267/317) say the primary segment is asset management services with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108, so no AIF revenue, segment result/EBIT/EBITDA/PBT or PAT is disclosed. The only AIF-related figures on these pages are NAM-India's own balance-sheet investments — 'Equity (AIF Schemes + Others)' in the Investment Book (e.g. INR 1,087 mn at Mar 31, 2026; INR 1,312 mn at Sep 30, 2026) and Level 2/3 fair-value holdings of Alternative Investment Funds — which are investment assets, not the AIF business's own revenue or profit.

years.source: Annual Report 2024 — page 231; Annual Report 2024 — page 285 (segment information: no separate reportable segment)
Annual Report 2025 — page 246; Annual Report 2025 — page 296 (segment information: no separate reportable segment)
Annual Report 2026 — page 267; Annual Report 2026 — page 317 (segment information: no separate reportable segment)

latest_quarter.source: Presentation Oct 2026 — page 36 (Investment Book shows only 'Equity (AIF Schemes + Others)' INR 1,312 mn as on Sep 30, 2026 — an investment holding, not AIF business revenue or profit)

verdict.not_found: All AIF-business figures: revenue, operating profit/segment result, PAT, AUM and quarterly numbers. Pages carry only group-level segment notes disclaiming separate segments and NAM-India's own AIF investment holdings.

verdict.rationale: The "separation" is Akzo Nobel India's carve-out of two units to its then-parent — the Powder Coatings business division (Interpon) and the Bangalore International Research Centre (IRC) — done as two slump sales under separate business transfer agreements concluded 1 July 2025, paired with the reverse purchase into the listed entity of all decorative-paints IPRs including the Dulux brand for India, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal at INR 11,520 million. The trigger was AkzoNobel NV's October 2024 strategic portfolio review "with initial focus on Deco South Asia", whose stated intent was to redeploy capital into the group's core; management said India was outperforming the industry and "in the sweet spot", yet there was a "strategic mismatch between the group's priorities versus the India operation". The parent, not the Indian board, initiated it: it came back in early January 2025 asking to buy Powder Coatings and IRC and to sell the decorative IP down to the listed company, which the board then notified and worked up via KMP, with KPMG and Grant Thornton (two SEBI-registered valuers) engaged on the Audit Chair's suggestion. Powder was retained globally because AkzoNobel is world market leader there with share twice the #2 player and "distinctive technology, raw materials" it wanted kept internal, and because it is severable — no technology dependency, different manufacturing process and largely separate facilities (Bangalore, Thane, Gwalior); a 36-month non-compete by AkzoNobel NV was attached. IRC was a captive cost centre doing 99% of its work for the global automotive and specialty coatings unit (colour development, McLaren Mercedes F1 colour testing), "they don't do anything for India", India's own business R&D labs being separate, with only a ~12% markup realised in the listed entity. Valuations: powder at INR 20.7 billion (~24.5x trailing EBITDA on a business that is ~10% of the company), IRC at INR 700 million (range 579–700), decorative IP at INR 11.5 billion on royalty relief (3% of decorative revenue, ~INR 68–69 crore of royalty, plus a 5-year growth assumption of ~11%); management said it took "the highest of what we sell and the lowest of what we buy… best for the minority shareholders", yielding ~INR 990 crore pre-tax inflow (tax ~14%) that was returned to shareholders as dividend. The deeper commercial logic management gave: as an MNC subsidiary measured on EBIT%/EBITDA% rather than absolutes, run on "global pricing modules", Dulux sat 5–9% above market (7–9% in premium/super-premium), could not play mass, economy, putty, mid-market or construction chemicals, and lacked "firepower" — owning the brand outright ends the royalty (~INR 60–65 crore p.a., explicitly redeployed into growth) and made the deco business cleanly saleable to a local owner, JSW Paints, which took 61.2% on 10 December 2025, ICIL selling its residual ~9% block for INR 1,296.09 crore on 17 December 2025. This repeats the 2017-18 chemicals divestment playbook — sell non-core to focus on paints and coatings — after which EBIT went from 8.8% (FY18) to 13.9% (FY24) and EPS from 44 to 94.
verdict.evolution: On the Nov 2024 call the review was only a parent-level process management was recused from, with "everything… in and all options" open; by the Feb 7, 2025 call the specific request to carve out Powder Coatings and the IRC had arrived from "the globe" and was explained as keeping liquid and powder as two distinct businesses. The 24 Feb 2025 binding offer was then priced and defended at the Mar 7, 2025 group meeting (two valuers, powder 24.5x EBITDA, IP via royalty relief), approved by shareholders (IP on 2 April 2025), cleared by Akzo's Supervisory Board on 12 June 2025 and closed 1 July 2025, with proceeds paid out as dividend (May/Aug 2025 calls). By the Nov 2025 call it was a restated-comparables exercise; the Feb 2026 call added an unflagged extra ~INR 200 crore of revenue (coil-coating customers, Acotone colorant exports) retained by the unlisted Akzo entity and quantified the INR 60–65 crore royalty saving, and by May 2026 the stated payoff was pricing freedom — 9.7% of price increases, premiums cut, 23% volume growth under JSW Dulux.

points.point: The review was parent-driven from the start; the Indian CEO and CFO recused themselves from the process AkzoNobel NV was anchoring, and no scope (deco vs coatings) was fixed.
points.quote: I want to be very clear that given the responsibilities of the role that I have, Krishna and myself are completely recused from the process that Akzo Nobel N.V., the parent company is sort of actually anchoring at this point of time.

points.point: Management said the carve-out request for Powder Coatings and the R&D centre came from the global parent, was brought first to the Board and then notified to the exchanges, and was "very initial thoughts… not final".
points.quote: But again, to answer this question, this is a request which has come from the globe, and we've been upfront as in the spirit of true governance to immediately notify first to bring it to the Board, inform the Board and the Board has then asked to notify to the stock exchanges, which we've done.

points.point: The purpose was framed as repositioning the Indian deco business to win locally, because the global parent judged that competing against Birla Opus-scale aggression needed "a local hand" rather than global investment discipline.
points.quote: The purpose of the strategic review, if you look at what Greg said, our global CEO, is to take AkzoNobel India to the winning position for various reasons, right?

points.point: Stated rationale: AkzoNobel NV's October 2024 portfolio review existed to redeploy capital into its core paints and coatings, with initial focus on South Asia.
points.quote: as you are aware in October '24, AkzoNobel has announced that its intention to do a strategic portfolio review, which was disclosed to the stock exchanges. And the intent of that review is to redeploy the capital towards growing its core paint and coatings business.

points.point: The explicit problem the separation solves: India was outperforming, but its priorities and the group's did not match — so ownership, not performance, was the issue.
points.quote: At the same time, there is a strategic mismatch between the group's priorities versus the India operation.

points.point: Powder Coatings was kept by the parent because AkzoNobel is global #1 there with share twice the #2 player and holds distinctive technology and raw materials it wants internal.
points.quote: So look, I think powder coatings we are designed to keep it, because globally we are a market leader with a market share twice the number two player.

points.point: The IRC went because it was a captive cost centre serving the global automotive and specialty coatings unit (colour development, McLaren Mercedes F1 testing), not India; India's business R&D labs are separate, and ~INR 50 crore had been spent on it.
points.quote: And along with that, we also told them to keep the R&D centre because it's a cost centre which only does 99% of the work for the global paint, automotive and specialty coatings business unit. And they don't do anything for India.

points.point: Separability was asserted on operations as well as strategy: powder shares no technology, process or (largely) facilities with the retained liquid-coatings businesses across Bangalore, Thane and Gwalior.
points.quote: There's no dependency in technologies, with completely different manufacturing process.

points.point: Pricing was defended on minority-shareholder grounds: powder valued at INR 20.7 billion (~24.5x trailing EBITDA, ~10% of the company), IRC at the top of its DCF range, deco IP at the bottom of its range — two SEBI-registered valuers (KPMG, Grant Thornton), reports available to shareholders on request.
points.quote: So we've taken the highest of what we sell and the lowest of what we buy. Because we said that's the best for the minority shareholders, right?

points.point: IRC valuation mechanics: discounted cash flow, range INR 579–700 million, highest taken; the unit was a cost-plus pass-through to the Netherlands with ~12% markup.
points.quote: Coming to the valuation of R&D centre, it came landed between the it's a discounted cash flow method and landed between 579 to 700 million, took the highest of that thing.

points.point: The Dulux/deco IP was bought in perpetuity (India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, including knowledge transfer), valued by royalty relief on the 3% royalty then paid.
points.quote: Presently, we do pay a royalty of around 3% of the revenue. Post this approval and the execution of the transaction, we need not have to pay any royalty.

points.point: A 36-month non-compete was taken from AkzoNobel NV on powder coatings; no non-compete arose on deco because the parent still held 75% of the listed entity at the time.
points.quote: The Powder Coatings business is concerned. Business transfer agreement would be AkzoNobel India Limited as it's divesting the powder coatings though AkzoNobel NV would not be participating in the powder coatings business for the next 36 months post execution.

points.point: Management positioned this as a repeat of the 2017-18 chemicals divestment playbook — shed non-core, focus on paints and coatings — citing 6% revenue CAGR, EBIT from 8.8% (FY18) to 13.9% (FY24), EPS 44 to 94 and INR 13.8bn / INR 303 per share of dividends.
points.quote: previously last time we came to the investors, seeking their special approval in terms of mandate is that in 2017-18, and we intended to diverse the chemicals business with their objective to focus on the core of the paints and coatings businesses.

points.point: Proceeds use was pre-committed to shareholders: sale consideration for powder and IRC, net of the deco IP/Dulux purchase price and net of tax, was paid out as dividend (on top of the INR 70/share 70th-anniversary special dividend), with policy allowing 85% of retained profits.
points.quote: once the AkzoNobel decided to buy out the powder coating and the IRC business, net of the IP rights and the brand Dulux rights that we have got, net of the taxes is the dividend that has got distributed amongst all the shareholders in toto.

points.point: Interpon (powder) was confirmed sold to AkzoNobel Global into a separate unlisted Indian company, and that sale is what funded the shareholder payout; International, Sikkens and Vehicle Refinish stay Akzo-owned but are made and sold by the new entity.
points.quote: Interpon is a powder coating product which has now been a part of the transaction where we have sold it to AkzoNobel Global, which is the reason why we got the money and the dividend that we were able to give.

points.point: The structural constraint the separation removes, stated plainly and attributed to the global CEO too: MNC ownership optimises margin percentages, not absolute profit, which capped investment behind Dulux.
points.quote: The global firms are constrained by percentages, percent margin, percent EBITDA, right, not absolutes which Indian firms look at.

points.point: Mechanics confirmed: February 2025 binding offer from AkzoNobel NV, postal-ballot shareholder approval, two separate business transfer agreements, both slump sales concluded 1 July 2025, so Q2 FY26 excludes Powder Coatings and IRC service income and last year was restated.
points.quote: As you are all aware, in February '25, we accepted the binding offer from AkzoNobel NV for the purchase of our Power Coatings business and International Research Center.

points.point: Scope was wider than the two named divisions: a further ~INR 200 crore of annual revenue (a couple of coil-coating customers, plus Dramatone/Acotone colorant exports to Southeast Asia and the Middle East) was retained by the unlisted AkzoNobel Powder Coatings India entity — ~INR 25 crore a quarter of lost revenue.
points.quote: there are certain other elements of the business which also got retained by the AkzoNobel Powder Coatings India private limited entity which is an unlisted company by the earlier parent, which includes specifically a couple of customers in the coil coating business.

points.point: The quantified benefit of the IP leg: decorative royalty ceased, worth roughly INR 60–65 crore a year, committed to growth initiatives and market share; industrial-coatings royalty continues to AkzoNobel as technology partner.
points.quote: In the month of June 2025, we acquired the decorative IP, and the Dulux brand is now owned by Akzo Nobel India Limited listed entity. So, the royalty ceased to exist which translates to roughly around 60 crores to 65 crores depending on the revenue trajectory.

points.point: Trade had been asking for the pricing freedom for years; it was impossible under Akzo's global pricing modules, and the company was "completely off" market operating prices, 5–9% overpriced, which had caused volume erosion.
points.quote: This is something that the trade has been asking us for the last couple of years, it is just that our ability to do that with AkzoNobel was very difficult because Akzo runs on global pricing modules.

points.point: Post-separation payoff as management framed it: premiums of 7–9% cut because the old parent measured EBIT%/EBITDA%, driving 23% blended volume growth against 6.2% revenue growth, EBITDA held ~14.4%.
points.quote: We were having premiums of almost close to 7% to 9%, because our earlier parent Akzo Nobel, and we used to measure performances on EBIT percent and EBITDA percent or absolute and unfortunately, the market like India, that has always been the challenge.

points.point: Filing record of the reverse leg: board accepted a binding offer on 24 February 2025 for transfer of all decorative-paints IPRs for India, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal at INR 11,520 million; shareholders approved 2 April 2025, Akzo's Supervisory Board 12 June 2025, completed 1 July 2025 and capitalised as an indefinite-life intangible.
points.quote: On 24 February 2025, the Board of Directors of the Company had accepted a binding offer letter of even date from Akzo Nobel N.V. (Ultimate Holding Company) for the purchase and transfer of all intellectual property rights ("IPRs") in relation to the decorative paints business of the Company in India, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal by Akzo Nobel Coatings International B.V. at a purchase consideration of INR 11,520 million.

points.point: Accounting outcome of the carve-out: INR 18,925 million exceptional gain, INR 79 million impairment of plant rendered unusable by the slump sale, INR 104 million retention incentive, INR 2,704 million current tax on the sale and a INR 362 million deferred-tax charge on the capitalised IPRs.
points.quote: Profit from slump sale of Powder Coatings business division and the International Research Center division (net of directly attributable expenses) amounting to INR 18,925 million.

points.point: Lenders did not ask for the separation but now constrain any further one: JSW Paints' debenture trust deeds (INR 3,300 crore NCDs, 30 Oct 2025; INR 2,950 crore, 4 Nov 2026) make demerger, merger, slump sale, business transfer, asset disposal, security creation and new debt at JSW Dulux conditional on parameters or Debenture Trustee consent, "with the view towards value preservation".
points.quote: Further, if ANIL undertakes any Disposal of fixed assets other than as permitted under the terms of the DTD, it will result in occurrence of a monetisation event and the Issuer will be required to redeem such Debentures for an amount equivalent to the aggregate proceeds received as consideration from such Disposal.

verdict.what_management_expects: For the listed entity: Dulux owned in perpetuity, 3% royalty gone (INR 60–65 crore redeployed into growth and market share), ~INR 990 crore pre-tax proceeds returned as dividend, and freedom from global EBIT%-led pricing to chase volume at 14.5–15% EBITDA, moving from #4 toward #3. For AkzoNobel NV: keeps globally #1 powder technology and captive global R&D, capital redeployed to its core.
verdict.gaps: Why ~INR 200 crore of coil-coating customers and Acotone colorant exports stayed with Akzo; standalone powder/IRC margins; dividend-versus-reinvestment split; synergy quantum; the 36-month non-compete's logic.

verdict.segment_name: Powder Coatings business division and International Research Center division ("Powder and IRC", the carved-out / AkzoNobel-retained business)
verdict.unit: ₹ crore (quarterly presentations) / ₹ million (annual reports) — no figures for this business itself are given in either
verdict.measure_notes: No profit or revenue line exists for the carved-out business on the supplied pages. The annual reports (FY2024 p142-143/210, FY2025 p156-157/230, FY2026 p80/114) state there is only one reportable segment, "Paints", so no segment result/EBIT is disclosed for Powder Coatings or the International Research Centre. The presentations give only continuing-business and total-entity P&Ls (Revenue, GM, OPEX, EBITDA/EBIT, PBT, PAT, including unallocable corporate items), with LY figures 'restated to exclude Powder and IRC contribution (provisional, unaudited, based on Mgmt estimates)'; the carved-out business's own revenue/profit is not shown and would have to be derived by subtraction, which is not reported here. Related items that are disclosed, but are not the business's financials: sale consideration of ₹21,922 million for the Powder Coatings and International Research Center divisions (Annual Report 2026 — page 81) and pre-tax exceptional proceeds of ₹1,874.2 crore / ₹18.7 bn from that sale in Q2 FY26 (Presentation Nov 2026 — page 13; Presentation Nov 2025 — page 7).

verdict.not_found: All of them: no revenue, EBITDA/EBIT or PAT for the Powder Coatings/IRC business in any year or quarter. Only entity totals, continuing-business restatements, sale consideration (₹21,922 mn) and exceptional gain (₹1,874.2 cr) are disclosed.

verdict.what_is_spun: Buildnext, a home design and project management services associate, swapped to JSW One for JSW One shares
demerged_business_names: home design and project management services
JSW One Platforms Limited (acquirer, whose shares Pidilite receives)

verdict.rationale: On the record supplied, the "separation" is not a new divestiture announced by NMDC Steel Limited (NSL, scrip NSLNISP / BSE 543768 / CSE 74920) — it is the already-completed demerger of the NISP business (NMDC Iron & Steel Plant, Nagarnar, Dist. Bastar, Chhattisgarh, a 3 MTPA-class greenfield integrated plant) out of NMDC Ltd., the iron-ore mining parent, into NSL as the "Resulting Company" (CIN L27310CT2015GOI001618). The stated reason is entirely a Government of India privatisation mechanic, not an operating or synergy argument: the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval on 27 October 2016 for strategic disinvestment of several CPSEs including the NISP unit of NMDC Ltd., and then on 14 October 2020 approved the demerger of NISP from NMDC together with strategic disinvestment of the resulting entity by selling the entire GoI stake. In other words, the carve-out exists so that the steel plant could be made a separately listed, separately saleable entity, leaving NMDC Ltd. as a pure mining company; the asker is the sovereign owner through CCEA, not investors, lenders or a JV partner. The transaction terms set out in the Preliminary Information Memorandum and the Request for Expression of Interest are that GoI divests 50.79% of NSL along with management control to a strategic buyer, and will additionally offer 10% of NSL to NMDC Ltd. once the strategic buyer has been identified through the bidding process. The scheme also allocated legacy exposure to the parent: the Rs 111.19 Cr GST input-credit dispute for July 2017–March 2021 (Rs 8.45 Cr paid, Rs 45.90 Cr dropped, Rs 56.40 Cr in abeyance before the Bilaspur High Court, Rs 0.35 Cr under appeal) is pre-demerger, so NMDC Ltd. files the appeals "as per the demerger scheme." Nothing in the filings claims the separation improves margins, capital allocation or valuation; the only measurable consequence disclosed is that standing alone cost NSL its parent's credit umbrella — rating fell from AAA to A- on demerger (NCD coupon 7.30% to 8.80% from 16.02.2023), then to BBB+ (9.05% from 5 June 2024), with the Rs 523.80 Cr NCDs rated "ICRA BBB+ Rating Watch with Developing Implications" and Ind A-/Negative until redemption on 28.08.2025, and the SBI rupee term loan of Rs 4,476.20 Cr (drawn Rs 4,475.81 Cr) repricing off external rating from 7.1% to 12.45% w.e.f. 01.03.2025 before being repositioned at NSL's request to 8.70% (12.04.2025), 8.45% (12.10.2025) and 8.40% (12.01.2026). Financially the standalone entity moved from a FY25 loss before tax of Rs 3,321.72 Cr on revenue of Rs 8,503.05 Cr (PAT Rs -2,373.78 Cr, EPS -8.10) to FY26 revenue of Rs 13,641.81 Cr with PBT Rs 75.78 Cr and PAT Rs 58.72 Cr, and Q1 FY27 (quarter ended 30.06.2026) revenue Rs 3,661.84 Cr with PBT Rs 73.95 Cr, PAT Rs 50.51 Cr, borrowings Rs 5,056.15 Cr and net worth Rs 13,228.35 Cr — i.e. the asset was handed to the market loss-making and has only just crossed into profit as the sale process remains open.
verdict.evolution: There are no earnings-call transcripts on file, so the only visible evolution is the repetition of the same two-step CCEA history — 27 October 2016 (in-principle strategic disinvestment of the NISP unit) and 14 October 2020 (demerger of NISP from NMDC plus sale of the entire GoI stake in the resulting entity) — carried verbatim as a note in each of the three filings dated 3 February 2026, 29 May 2026 and 14/15 August 2026, with the PIM/EoI terms (50.79% plus control to a strategic buyer, 10% offered to NMDC Ltd. afterwards) unchanged throughout. What changes across the three is the aftermath rather than the plan: by the 3 February 2026 filing the Rs 523.80 Cr NCDs had been redeemed on 28.08.2025 (principal plus Rs 42.98 Cr interest, net of Rs 4.42 Cr TDS), ending the "Rating Watch with Developing Implications" overhang, and the SBI term loan had been stepped down from the 12.45% post-DCCO reset to 8.45%. By the 14 August 2026 filing the rate is 8.40% (from 12.01.2026), term-loan outstanding is Rs 3,177.27 Cr after Rs 1,298.54 Cr repaid, and the entity is profitable (Q1 FY27 PAT Rs 50.51 Cr) — but no filing records any new stage of the sale, bidder shortlist or revised structure. No fresh separation is announced by NSL in this window; the company reports a single segment and no subsidiaries, JVs or associates.

points.point: Filings of 03.02.2026, 29.05.2026 and 14.08.2026 all trace the separation to CCEA's 27 October 2016 in-principle approval for strategic disinvestment of CPSEs including the NISP unit of NMDC Ltd. — i.e. the sale decision predates the carve-out.
points.quote: Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs ("CCEA"), in its meeting dated October 27, 2016, gave in-principle approval for strategic disinvestment ("Strategic Disinvestment") of several CPSEs including the NISP unit of NMDC Ltd.

points.point: The demerger itself was approved on 14 October 2020 expressly as the vehicle for selling the Government's entire holding in the resulting entity — separation as a privatisation enabler, not an operating restructuring.
points.quote: Subsequently, on October 14, 2020, CCEA gave its 'in­principle' approval to the demerger of NISP from NMDC and strategic disinvestment of the resulting entity by selling entire stake of Government of India ("Gol").
